questions.stem: A calcium atom has 20 protons. In calcium chloride, calcium is present as a particle containing 20 protons and 18 electrons. Which statement best describes how the bond in this compound forms?

options.text: Two atoms share a pair of valence electrons unequally, producing partial charges but no full ions.
Two atoms share one pair of valence electrons equally, so neither atom ends up carrying any charge.
One atom transfers valence electrons to another, and the resulting oppositely charged ions attract electrostatically.
Fixed metal cations are held in place by a sea of delocalized electrons shared among all the atoms.

rationales.whyCorrect: An ionic bond is the electrostatic attraction between a cation and an anion generated by electron transfer, typically from a metal of low ionization energy to a nonmetal of high electron affinity. A particle with 20 protons and 18 electrons carries a net charge of 20 - 18 = 2+, confirming that calcium has lost two electrons; each chlorine gains one, becoming Cl-. Option B describes a nonpolar covalent bond, option A a polar covalent bond, and option D metallic bonding, none of which involves the full charge separation seen here.
rationales.eli10: Charge is just a proton-versus-electron headcount. Calcium normally has 20 of each, so it is neutral. Hand two electrons away and it still has 20 protons but only 18 electrons, leaving it two positive units short of balanced: Ca2+. The chlorine atoms that caught those electrons each end up one unit negative. Opposite charges pull on each other, and that pull between transferred-electron ions is the ionic bond.

questions.stem: In an H2 molecule the two hydrogen atoms are joined by a single covalent bond, which consists of 1 shared pair, or 2 electrons. Which statement correctly defines a covalent bond?

options.text: The attraction of a cation for an anion within a repeating three-dimensional crystal lattice.
The mutual attraction of two nuclei for the same pair or pairs of shared valence electrons.
The attraction between the partially positive end of one molecule and the partially negative end of another.
The attraction of fixed metal cations for valence electrons that move freely throughout the solid.

rationales.whyCorrect: A covalent bond exists because both positively charged nuclei are simultaneously attracted to the same region of electron density concentrated between them; that shared density lowers the potential energy of the system relative to the separated atoms. A single bond holds 1 pair x 2 electrons = 2 electrons. Option A defines ionic bonding, option C describes dipole-dipole attraction between separate molecules, and option D describes metallic bonding.
rationales.eli10: A covalent bond is not one atom capturing an electron; it is two nuclei pulling on the same electrons at once. Put a pair of electrons in the space between two hydrogen nuclei and each nucleus is attracted to that negative cloud. Neither can pull away without giving up that attraction, so the atoms stay joined. One shared pair equals 2 electrons equals one single bond, which is exactly what holds H2 together.

questions.stem: Which example is best classified as an ionic compound, and how many ions are present in one of its formula units?

options.text: MgCl2, which contains 3 ions per formula unit
CO2, which contains 3 ions per formula unit
CH4, which contains 5 ions per formula unit
N2, which contains 2 ions per formula unit

rationales.whyCorrect: Ionic compounds typically form between a metal and a nonmetal; MgCl2 consists of one Mg2+ cation and two Cl- anions, giving 1 + 2 = 3 ions per formula unit. CH4, CO2, and N2 are molecular substances built entirely from nonmetal atoms joined by shared electron pairs, so they contain no ions at all, and counting their atoms is not the same as counting ions. Screening a formula for metal-plus-nonmetal composition is the fastest first test for ionic character.
rationales.eli10: Use a two-step sort. First, look for a metal paired with a nonmetal: magnesium is a metal and chlorine is not, so MgCl2 is ionic, while carbon, hydrogen, oxygen, and nitrogen are all nonmetals, making the other three molecular. Second, count charged pieces, not atoms. MgCl2 breaks into one Mg2+ and two Cl-, which is three ions. CH4 has five atoms but zero ions, which is the trap in that option.

questions.stem: Sodium chloride melts near 801 degrees C, while methane melts near -182 degrees C, a difference of 983 degrees C. What is the primary reason for this very large gap?

options.text: Melting sodium chloride breaks a lattice of strong ion-ion attractions, while melting methane overcomes only weak intermolecular forces.
Melting methane breaks the strong C-H covalent bonds inside each molecule, while melting sodium chloride leaves its ionic bonds fully intact.
Melting sodium chloride overcomes many weak attractions that add up, while melting methane breaks one unusually strong covalent bond.
Sodium chloride is built from much heavier atoms than methane, so far more thermal energy is needed to set its particles moving.

rationales.whyCorrect: In an ionic solid each ion is attracted to every oppositely charged neighbor throughout a continuous three-dimensional array, so melting must supply enough energy to overcome a large lattice energy. Methane is a molecular solid whose discrete molecules are held to one another only by weak London dispersion forces; melting separates the molecules while the strong C-H covalent bonds inside each molecule remain untouched. Option B reverses which particles come apart, option C wrongly treats the ionic lattice as a stack of weak additive attractions and methane as having a single covalent bond, and option D misattributes the gap to atomic mass rather than to the type of force being broken.
rationales.eli10: Melting always asks the same question: what has to let go for particles to start sliding past each other? In sodium chloride the answer is full positive-negative attractions running through the whole crystal, which is a lot to overcome. In methane the answer is only the faint stickiness between separate molecules; the bonds inside each CH4 stay put. Weak attractions give way at -182 degrees C, strong ionic ones not until 801 degrees C, a melting temperature 983 degrees C higher.

questions.stem: Using Pauling electronegativity values (H = 2.2, Cl = 3.16), the H-Cl bond has an electronegativity difference of 0.96. Which classification of this bond, with its consequence, is correct?

options.text: Nonpolar covalent, because the electrons are shared equally and no partial charges develop.
Ionic, because chlorine removes hydrogen's electron completely, so an isolated HCl molecule consists of H+ and Cl- ions.
Polar covalent, because the shared pair sits closer to chlorine, giving chlorine a partial negative and hydrogen a partial positive charge.
Coordinate covalent, because chlorine supplies both electrons of the shared pair while hydrogen supplies none.

rationales.whyCorrect: An electronegativity difference of roughly 0.4 to 1.7 marks a polar covalent bond: the pair is genuinely shared, but unequally. At 3.16 - 2.2 = 0.96, chlorine draws the bonding pair closer and carries a partial negative charge (delta minus) while hydrogen carries a partial positive charge (delta plus), giving HCl a permanent dipole moment. Complete transfer to separate ions requires a much larger difference, which is why gaseous HCl is a polar molecule rather than an ionic solid. In HCl each atom contributes one electron to the bond, so it is not coordinate covalent.
rationales.eli10: Bond polarity is about where the shared electrons spend their time, not about who owns them. Chlorine's electronegativity of 3.16 beats hydrogen's 2.2 by 0.96, so the pair is pulled toward the chlorine side without ever leaving hydrogen entirely. The result is a molecule with a slightly negative chlorine end and a slightly positive hydrogen end, written delta minus and delta plus. Partial charges like these, not full ionic charges, are the signature of a polar covalent bond.

questions.stem: A neutral nitrogen atom has 5 valence electrons and reaches an octet of 8 by sharing. How many covalent bonds does nitrogen typically form, and why?

options.text: Three, because sharing three pairs supplies the 3 additional electrons nitrogen needs to reach 8.
Four, because nitrogen has four valence orbitals available and places one bond in each of them.
Five, because an atom forms one covalent bond for every valence electron that it already possesses.
None, because nitrogen's 5 valence electrons already give it a stable half-filled outer shell.

rationales.whyCorrect: For a neutral main-group atom, the usual number of covalent bonds equals the number of electrons short of an octet: 8 - 5 = 3 for nitrogen. Each shared pair counts toward the octets of both bonded atoms, so three bonds bring nitrogen's count from 5 to 8 while leaving one lone pair, as in NH3 or the triple bond of N2. Option B applies carbon's pattern to nitrogen, option C confuses electrons owned with electrons needed, and option D misapplies half-filled subshell stability, which describes relative ionization trends rather than an atom's tendency to bond.
rationales.eli10: Ask how many electrons the atom is missing, not how many it has. Nitrogen holds 5 valence electrons and an octet needs 8, so it is short by 3. Every covalent bond lets nitrogen count one more electron from a partner toward its own octet, so three bonds close the gap exactly. That leaves the remaining two electrons as a lone pair, which is why ammonia is N with three H atoms plus one lone pair rather than four or five bonds.

questions.stem: Solid sodium chloride does not conduct electricity, but 0.5 mol of it dissolved in water releases a total of 1 mol of ions. What happens to the electrical conductivity of the sample, and why?

options.text: It conducts electricity, because dissolving breaks covalent bonds and releases free electrons into the water.
It conducts electricity, because dissolving frees the Na+ and Cl- ions to move independently and carry charge.
It does not conduct electricity, because intact NaCl molecules simply spread out among the water molecules.
It conducts only once molten, because water molecules surround the ions and neutralize their charges.

rationales.whyCorrect: Conduction in solution requires mobile charge carriers. In the crystal the ions are charged but locked into fixed lattice sites; dissolution (like melting) releases them so Na+ and Cl- can migrate toward opposite electrodes, making NaCl a strong electrolyte. Each formula unit supplies 2 ions, so 0.5 mol x 2 = 1 mol of ions. NaCl contains no discrete molecules and releases no free electrons, and hydration shells stabilize ionic charge rather than cancel it.
rationales.eli10: Electric current is charge in motion, so a substance needs charges that are both present and free to travel. Solid salt has the charges but not the freedom, since every ion is pinned in the lattice, so it is an insulator. Water surrounds each ion and pulls the lattice apart, and now those charges can drift toward electrodes and carry current. Because every NaCl unit yields two ions, 0.5 mol of salt sets 1 mol of charge carriers loose. Dissolved electrolytes are also why body fluids conduct the signals an ECG records.

questions.stem: In carbon dioxide, carbon is joined to each oxygen by a double bond, so the two double bonds account for 8 bonding electrons in a linear O=C=O arrangement. Which statement about bonding and polarity in CO2 is correct?

options.text: The bonds are ionic, because oxygen pulls the bonding electrons completely away from carbon.
Each C=O bond is polar, but the linear symmetric geometry makes the two bond dipoles cancel.
The molecule is polar overall, because each oxygen atom carries a partial negative charge.
Both C=O bonds are nonpolar, because carbon and oxygen attract the shared electrons equally.

rationales.whyCorrect: Oxygen (3.44) is considerably more electronegative than carbon (2.55), so every C=O bond carries a dipole. Bond dipoles are vectors, however: in a linear, symmetric molecule the two equal dipoles point in opposite directions and sum to a net dipole moment of zero, so CO2 is a nonpolar molecule built from polar bonds. Molecular polarity therefore depends on geometry as well as bond polarity. The bonding framework is covalent, not ionic, and the electron count confirms it: 2 double bonds x 4 electrons = 8 bonding electrons.
rationales.eli10: Treat each polar bond as an arrow pointing toward the more electronegative atom. In CO2 the molecule is a straight line with an oxygen on each end, so the two arrows have equal length and point exactly opposite ways, and they add to zero. The bonds are still polar, and the oxygens really do carry partial negative charge, but the molecule as a whole has no positive end or negative end. Bend that same arrangement, as in water, and the arrows stop cancelling and the molecule becomes polar.

questions.stem: Aluminum forms Al3+ ions and oxygen forms O2- ions. Which formula for the compound they produce, together with its reasoning, is correct?

options.text: Al3O2, because each element's subscript is set equal to the size of that element's own charge.
AlO, because every ionic compound pairs one cation with one anion in a 1:1 ratio.
Al2O3, because the total positive charge (2 x 3+ = 6+) exactly balances the total negative charge (3 x 2- = 6-).
Al2O3, because each aluminum atom shares three pairs of electrons with each oxygen atom.

rationales.whyCorrect: An ionic formula gives the lowest whole-number ratio of ions that makes the compound electrically neutral. Two Al3+ contribute 2 x 3 = 6 units of positive charge and three O2- contribute 6 units of negative charge, so the formula is Al2O3. Option B assumes a universal 1:1 ratio, which holds only when the ion charges are equal in magnitude (as in NaCl). Option A copies each charge onto its own element instead of crossing it over, and option D gives the right formula with covalent reasoning, even though a metal oxide of this type is ionic.
rationales.eli10: Neutrality is the rule that sets every ionic formula. Each Al3+ adds 3 positive units and each O2- adds 2 negative units, so you need the smallest counts that make the totals match: two aluminums give 6 positive and three oxides give 6 negative, hence Al2O3. The crossover shortcut works because it lands on that same balance, but only if you cross the charges over, writing oxygen's 2 as aluminum's subscript and aluminum's 3 as oxygen's subscript, then reducing if possible.

questions.stem: A student looks up Pauling electronegativity values for potassium (0.82) and bromine (2.96) to predict the bonding in potassium bromide. Which interpretation of these data is best supported?

options.text: The difference is about 3.78, so the bond is ionic because the two electronegativity values add together.
The difference is about 2.14, so the bond is nonpolar covalent because both atoms are relatively large.
The difference is about 2.14, so the bond is polar covalent; the shared pair stays roughly midway between the two nuclei.
The difference is about 2.14, so the bond is largely ionic; potassium's valence electron transfers to bromine, forming K+ and Br- in a lattice.

rationales.whyCorrect: Electronegativity difference is found by subtraction, not addition: 2.96 - 0.82 = 2.14. Differences above roughly 1.7 to 2.0 indicate predominantly ionic character, which fits a group 1 metal combining with a halogen. The transferred electron yields K+ and Br-, and these ions assemble into an extended crystal lattice rather than discrete KBr molecules. Option A uses the wrong operation, option B ignores the size of the difference in favor of atomic radius, and option C pairs a very large difference with equal sharing, which is self-contradictory.
rationales.eli10: Electronegativity rates how strongly an atom pulls on shared electrons, so what matters is the gap between the two ratings, which means subtraction. Bromine at 2.96 against potassium at 0.82 leaves a gap of 2.14, well past the roughly 1.7 mark where sharing stops being realistic. At that point potassium does not merely lose the tug of war, it hands the electron over, producing K+ and Br- that stack into a salt crystal. Adding the values, as in option A, measures nothing meaningful.

questions.stem: In a teaching data set, breaking an O-H covalent bond inside a water molecule requires about 460 kJ/mol, while breaking a hydrogen bond between two water molecules requires about 20 kJ/mol. Which conclusion is best supported by this comparison?

options.text: Boiling water breaks its O-H covalent bonds, which is why steam is chemically different from liquid water.
Water's high boiling point reflects individual hydrogen bonds that are each only 23 kJ/mol weaker than an O-H bond.
A hydrogen bond is a weak covalent bond in which two molecules share one hydrogen atom's single electron.
The O-H bond is about 23 times stronger than the hydrogen bond, so boiling separates whole molecules without breaking O-H bonds.

rationales.whyCorrect: Dividing the two values gives 460 / 20 = 23, an order-of-magnitude gap between an intramolecular covalent bond and an intermolecular attraction. Vaporization supplies far less energy than 460 kJ/mol, so it overcomes only the weaker hydrogen bonds; steam is still H2O with its O-H bonds intact. Option C misdefines a hydrogen bond, which is a strong dipole-dipole attraction rather than a shared-electron bond. Option B misreads the data: the two energies differ by a factor of 23, not by 23 kJ/mol, since 460 - 20 = 440.
rationales.eli10: Read the numbers as a ratio, because that tells you which attraction gives way first. At 460 versus 20 kJ/mol, the covalent O-H bond is about 23 times harder to break than a hydrogen bond, so any process supplying modest energy attacks the hydrogen bonds and nothing else. Boiling is exactly that: molecules separate from one another and drift off intact, which is why steam is still water and not loose H and O atoms. Hydrogen bonds are weak individually, but a liquid holds so many of them that water still needs unusual amounts of heat to boil.

questions.stem: Ammonium sulfate, (NH4)2SO4, contains 15 atoms per formula unit and dissolves in water to give NH4+ and SO4 2- ions. Which statement best explains the bonding present in this compound?

options.text: Every bond in the compound is ionic, because the substance is a salt that separates into ions in water.
Every bond in the compound is covalent, because the formula contains only nonmetal atoms.
The N-H and S-O bonds are ionic, while the attraction between the two polyatomic ions is covalent.
Covalent bonds hold the atoms together within each polyatomic ion, while ionic attractions hold NH4+ and SO4 2- to one another.

rationales.whyCorrect: Compounds built from polyatomic ions display both bonding types at once: shared electron pairs bind N to H and S to O inside each ion, while electrostatic attraction between the resulting NH4+ and SO4 2- units builds the lattice. That is precisely why dissolution releases intact polyatomic ions instead of free N, H, S, and O atoms, ruling out option A. Option B ignores that a cation and an anion are present despite the all-nonmetal composition, and option C reverses the two bond types. Counting confirms the composition: 2 x (1 + 4) + 1 + 4 = 15 atoms per formula unit.
rationales.eli10: Polyatomic ions force you to look at two levels at once. Inside NH4+, nitrogen and hydrogen share electron pairs, and inside SO4 2-, sulfur and oxygen do the same, so those internal links are covalent and survive dissolving. Between the two clusters there is nothing shared at all, only a positive group attracted to a negative group, which is ionic. The all-nonmetal formula fools people into calling it purely covalent, but the ions in solution prove otherwise. Atom count: two NH4 groups give 2 x 5 = 10, plus one S and four O, for 15.

questions.stem: Which statement best defines the molar mass of a substance?

options.text: The mass in grams of one representative particle of the substance, read directly from an analytical balance
The mass in grams of one mole of the substance, numerically equal to its atomic or formula mass in amu
The combined count of protons and neutrons in one representative particle, expressed in atomic mass units
The volume in liters that one mole of the substance occupies at standard temperature and pressure

rationales.whyCorrect: Molar mass is the mass of exactly one mole (6.022 x 10^23 representative particles) of a substance, with units of grams per mole. Its numerical value matches the atomic mass (for elements) or the formula/molecular mass (for compounds) expressed in atomic mass units, which is why the periodic table can be read directly as a table of molar masses: for water, 2(1.008) + 15.999 = 18.015 g/mol. A single particle has a mass of only about 10^-23 g, and molar volume is a separate quantity that varies with phase, temperature, and pressure.
rationales.eli10: Weighing is easy; counting atoms is impossible. Molar mass is the trick that turns one into the other: it tells you what one mole-sized batch of particles weighs. The convenient part is that the number is already printed on the periodic table. Hydrogen reads 1.008 and oxygen reads 15.999, so one mole of water weighs 1.008 + 1.008 + 15.999 = 18.015 grams. Same number, two different scales: amu when you are talking about one particle, grams when you are talking about a mole of them.

questions.stem: Which value correctly states the number of representative particles contained in exactly one mole of any substance?

options.text: 6.022 x 10^23 particles, the value known as Avogadro's number that defines the mole
1.008 x 10^23 particles, since the mole is anchored to the molar mass of hydrogen
6.022 x 10^-23 particles, since the exponent is negative for quantities as small as atoms
1.204 x 10^24 particles, since the mole is referenced to a 12-gram sample of carbon-12

rationales.whyCorrect: The Avogadro constant is 6.02214076 x 10^23 mol^-1 (an exact defined value in the SI system since 2019), commonly rounded to 6.022 x 10^23. It applies to whatever the representative particle is: atoms for elements, molecules for molecular compounds, formula units for ionic compounds. Because the count is fixed, one mole of any substance contains the same number of particles even though the masses differ widely. A negative exponent would describe a fraction of a particle, and 12 g of carbon-12 contains one mole, not two.
rationales.eli10: A dozen always means 12, whether the items are eggs or bricks; only the weight changes. A mole always means 6.022 x 10^23, whether the items are gold atoms or water molecules. The number is enormous because atoms are so small that you need hundreds of thousands of billions of billions of them before the pile is big enough to see and weigh. Note the sign of the exponent: 10^23 is a huge count. A negative exponent would mean less than one particle, which cannot be what a mole means.

questions.stem: A laboratory sample contains 116.88 g of sodium chloride (molar mass 58.44 g/mol). How many moles of sodium chloride are present?

options.text: 0.5 mol, obtained by dividing the molar mass by the sample mass
2 mol, obtained by dividing the sample mass by the molar mass
58.44 mol, since the molar mass reports the mole count of the sample directly
6830 mol, obtained by multiplying the sample mass by the molar mass

rationales.whyCorrect: Moles are obtained by dividing the measured mass by the molar mass: 116.88 g / 58.44 g/mol = 2 mol. Dimensional analysis confirms the setup, because grams divided by grams per mole leaves moles. Option A inverts the ratio, giving 0.5 with units of mol^-1 (grams per mole divided by grams leaves 1/mol), and option D multiplies, giving about 6830 with units of g^2/mol; neither result carries the unit mol, so checking units catches both errors before the number is reported. Option C simply repeats the molar mass value and ignores the sample mass entirely.
rationales.eli10: If one sack of flour weighs 5 pounds and you are holding 10 pounds of flour, you have 10 / 5 = 2 sacks. Molar mass is the weight of one sack of particles, 58.44 g per mole for table salt, and your sample weighs 116.88 g. Divide and you get 2 sacks, meaning 2 moles. Carry the units through the arithmetic as a check: g divided by g/mol leaves mol, which is what the question asked for. If you divide or multiply the other way around, the leftover units are not moles, which is your signal to flip the setup and try again.

questions.stem: Two beakers each hold 100 g of solid: one holds glucose (180.16 g/mol) and the other holds water ice (18.02 g/mol). Which comparison of the two samples is accurate?

options.text: The two samples hold equal numbers of moles, since their masses are equal
The glucose sample holds about 10 times more moles, since its molar mass is larger
The two samples hold equal numbers of molecules, since molar mass affects only the mass
The water sample holds about 10 times more moles, since its molar mass is about 10 times smaller

rationales.whyCorrect: Moles equal mass divided by molar mass, so at fixed mass the mole count is inversely proportional to molar mass. Since 180.16 / 18.02 is about 9.998, the same 100 g yields roughly ten times as many moles of water as of glucose (about 5.55 mol versus 0.555 mol). Equal masses therefore do not imply equal mole counts or equal particle counts, which is precisely why chemists convert to moles before comparing amounts or setting up reactions.
rationales.eli10: Picture 100 grams of marbles beside 100 grams of bowling balls. The scale reads the same, but you have far more marbles because each one is light. A water molecule is the marble here at 18.02 g per mole, and a glucose molecule is the bowling ball at 180.16 g per mole, roughly ten times heavier. So the same 100 g gives you about ten times as many water molecules. Heavier particles means fewer of them in every gram.

questions.stem: The periodic table lists the molar mass of chlorine as 35.45 g/mol, yet no individual chlorine atom has that mass. What accounts for this non-whole-number value?

options.text: Electrons contribute a small fractional mass that pulls the value away from a whole number
It is the abundance-weighted average of the masses of chlorine's naturally occurring isotopes
It is the plain average of the mass numbers 35 and 37, since both isotopes occur in nature
It is the mass of a single chlorine-35 atom, rounded to two decimal places for tabulation

rationales.whyCorrect: Natural chlorine is about 75.76% chlorine-35 (34.969 amu) and 24.24% chlorine-37 (36.966 amu), giving (0.7576)(34.969) + (0.2424)(36.966) = 35.45 amu. Because any real sample is a mixture of isotopes, the tabulated atomic mass is an abundance-weighted average rather than the mass of any single atom. An unweighted average of 35 and 37 would give 36, electron mass is negligible at this precision, and 34.969 rounds to 34.97 rather than 35.45.
rationales.eli10: Suppose a group has 76 members weighing 35 kg and 24 members weighing 37 kg. The group average is about 35.5 kg, even though no single member weighs that. Chlorine is the same situation: most chlorine atoms are the lighter chlorine-35 type and a smaller share are chlorine-37. The periodic table reports the average, weighted so the more common isotope counts more heavily. Note that a plain average of 35 and 37 would give 36, so the weighting is what pulls chlorine's listed value down to 35.45.

questions.stem: Which comparison of 1 mol of neon gas and 1 mol of nitrogen gas (N2) is accurate?

options.text: Neon holds more representative particles, because its particles are single atoms rather than molecules
Nitrogen holds more representative particles, because each of its molecules is built from two atoms
Both hold the same number of representative particles, but the nitrogen sample holds twice as many atoms
Both hold the same number of atoms, because one mole fixes the atom count at 6.022 x 10^23

rationales.whyCorrect: One mole of any substance contains 6.022 x 10^23 representative particles, so both samples contain that count: atoms for neon, molecules for N2. Each N2 molecule holds two nitrogen atoms, so the nitrogen sample contains 2(6.022 x 10^23) = 1.2044 x 10^24 atoms while neon contains 6.022 x 10^23 atoms. Identifying the representative particle before converting is what prevents this very common error in mole-to-particle work.
rationales.eli10: A mole counts whatever unit the substance is made of. For neon the unit is a lone atom; for nitrogen gas the unit is a molecule of two bonded atoms. One mole of each gives the same number of units, like one dozen single socks versus one dozen pairs of socks. The dozens match, but the pairs contain twice as many actual socks. So 1 mol of N2 holds 6.022 x 10^23 molecules and 1.2044 x 10^24 nitrogen atoms. Always ask which particle the question wants counted.

questions.stem: What is the primary purpose of the mole concept in chemistry?

options.text: It links a countable number of particles to a mass that can be measured on a laboratory balance
It converts the volume of a liquid sample into its density without any mass measurement
It fixes the number of atoms written as subscripts when a chemical formula is constructed
It sets the volume that one mole of any liquid occupies, so samples can be compared by volume

rationales.whyCorrect: Substances react in whole-number particle ratios, yet no balance can count individual particles. The mole is the conversion bridge: molar mass turns a weighable mass into a particle count, so 0.25 mol of calcium carbonate (100.09 g/mol) corresponds to a measurable 25.02 g and to about 1.5 x 10^23 formula units. This macroscopic-to-microscopic link underpins stoichiometry, solution concentration, and clinical dosage calculations. Subscripts come from bonding and charge balance, and molar volume is a separate concept that applies mainly to gases.
rationales.eli10: You cannot count grains of rice before dinner, but you can weigh out a cup and know approximately how many you have. Chemists face the same problem in a harsher form, since atoms are far too small to count at all. So they weigh instead, and molar mass is the conversion card: one mole of this substance weighs this many grams. Need 0.25 mol of chalk? Weigh 25.02 g and you have counted about 1.5 x 10^23 formula units without counting anything.

questions.stem: A student measures out 9 g of pure water (18.02 g/mol) for a classroom demonstration. Approximately how many water molecules does this sample contain?

options.text: 3 x 10^23 molecules, obtained by converting to moles and then multiplying by Avogadro's number
1.2 x 10^24 molecules, obtained by doubling Avogadro's number for the two hydrogen atoms
5.4 x 10^24 molecules, obtained by multiplying the mass in grams by Avogadro's number
3.3 x 10^22 molecules, obtained by dividing Avogadro's number by the molar mass

rationales.whyCorrect: Mass-to-particle problems take two steps: 9 g / 18.02 g/mol = 0.4994 mol, then 0.4994 mol x 6.022 x 10^23 mol^-1 = 3.008 x 10^23 molecules. Multiplying grams by Avogadro's number without the mole step inflates the result by a factor of the molar mass, giving 5.4 x 10^24. The answer is reasonable because 9 g is about half of water's 18.02 g/mol, so the count should be about half of Avogadro's number.
rationales.eli10: Treat this as a two-leg trip with moles as the connecting stop. There is no direct route from grams to molecules. Leg one: 9 g divided by 18.02 g per mole is about half a mole. Leg two: half a mole times 6.022 x 10^23 particles per mole is about 3 x 10^23 molecules. The sanity check is quick, since half a mole should give half of Avogadro's number, and it does. Any answer larger than 10^24 for such a small sample means the mole step was skipped.

questions.stem: A chemistry exercise calls for preparing exactly 0.5 mol of glucose (C6H12O6, molar mass 180.16 g/mol). Which mass should be weighed out, and why?

options.text: 180.16 g, because the molar mass is the mass to weigh whenever a mole quantity is specified
360.32 g, because the molar mass is divided by the requested mole quantity
90.08 g, because mass equals the requested moles multiplied by the molar mass
0.00278 g, because the requested moles are divided by the molar mass

rationales.whyCorrect: Converting moles to mass uses mass = moles x molar mass, so 0.5 mol x 180.16 g/mol = 90.08 g. The units confirm the setup, since moles multiplied by grams per mole leaves grams. Dividing instead produces 360.32 g or 0.00278 g, both of which fail the estimation check that half a mole must weigh half of the molar mass.
rationales.eli10: If one full container of a substance weighs 180.16 grams, half a container weighs half that, which is 90.08 grams. That is the whole calculation: moles times molar mass. Build in the estimate before you compute. When the requested amount is less than one mole, the mass must come out smaller than the molar mass; when it is more than one mole, the mass must come out larger. An answer that breaks this rule means the multiplication was flipped into a division.

questions.stem: A hypothetical teaching solution is prepared by dissolving 11.1 g of calcium chloride, CaCl2 (110.98 g/mol), in water so that it fully dissociates. How many moles of chloride ions does the solution contain?

options.text: 0.05 mol, because the compound's moles are split evenly between the two kinds of ions
0.1 mol, because each formula unit releases one chloride ion into solution
2 mol, because the subscript 2 states the chloride mole quantity directly
0.2 mol, because each formula unit releases two chloride ions into solution

rationales.whyCorrect: First convert to moles of compound: 11.1 g / 110.98 g/mol = 0.1 mol CaCl2. The formula shows two chloride ions per formula unit, so the ratio of 2 mol Cl- per 1 mol CaCl2 gives 0.2 mol chloride (alongside 0.1 mol Ca2+). Subscripts in a formula are per-unit ratios, not absolute mole quantities, which is the misconception behind the 2 mol option.
rationales.eli10: Each CaCl2 formula unit arrives as a set: one calcium ion and two chloride ions, like a bicycle with one frame and two wheels. Weighing tells you the number of sets, here 0.1 mole of them. The number of wheels is twice that, so 0.2 mole of chloride. The subscript 2 never means two moles on its own; it means two per unit. The order matters: find moles of the whole compound first, then apply the subscript as a multiplier.

questions.stem: A 21.5 g sample of a purified unknown compound is determined to contain 0.25 mol of that compound. What is its molar mass, and what does this value represent?

options.text: 5.375 g/mol, representing the mass contributed by each individual molecule in the sample
0.0116 g/mol, representing the fraction of a mole contained in each gram of the sample
21.5 g/mol, representing the mass of the sample reported on a per-mole basis
86 g/mol, representing the mass of 6.022 x 10^23 molecules of the compound

rationales.whyCorrect: Molar mass is mass divided by moles: 21.5 g / 0.25 mol = 86 g/mol. Conceptually that is the mass of one full mole, meaning 6.022 x 10^23 molecules of the compound. Determining molar mass this way reverses the usual conversion and is how an unknown is identified once its empirical formula is known, since the molecular formula must be a whole-number multiple of the empirical formula mass.
rationales.eli10: You have a quarter of a container and it weighs 21.5 grams, so a full container weighs four times as much, which is 86 grams. Molar mass is that full-container weight, where a full container means 6.022 x 10^23 molecules. Dividing by 0.25 is the same as multiplying by 4, so watch the direction: the answer must be larger than 21.5 g, because a whole mole always outweighs a quarter of one. Options smaller than 21.5 g can be ruled out before any arithmetic.

questions.stem: Four sealed vials each contain exactly 1 g of a pure gas: hydrogen (H2, 2.016 g/mol), helium (He, 4.003 g/mol), nitrogen (N2, 28.02 g/mol), and oxygen (O2, 32 g/mol). Which vial contains the greatest total number of atoms?

options.text: The oxygen vial, because its larger molar mass supplies more atomic material per gram
The helium vial, because single atoms give more particles per gram than bonded molecules do
The hydrogen vial, because it has both the smallest molar mass and two atoms per molecule
The nitrogen vial, because its molar mass balances particle count against atoms per molecule

rationales.whyCorrect: At fixed mass, moles rise as molar mass falls, and the total atom count then scales with the atoms per formula unit. Hydrogen gives (1 g / 2.016 g/mol) x 2 = 0.992 mol of atoms, compared with 0.25 mol for helium, 0.0714 mol for nitrogen, and 0.0625 mol for oxygen. Being monatomic does not help helium enough, since each helium atom is nearly twice the mass of an entire H2 molecule, so the diatomic gas still wins on both factors combined.
rationales.eli10: Two factors decide atoms per gram: how light each particle is, and how many atoms each particle carries. Hydrogen leads on both. It is the lightest molecule there is, so 1 g gives about half a mole of molecules, and each molecule carries two atoms, doubling that to about 0.992 mole of atoms. Helium comes as single atoms, which sounds like an advantage, but one helium atom outweighs a whole H2 molecule, so 1 g yields only 0.25 mole of atoms. Lightest plus doubled beats single but heavier.

questions.stem:
What is the molar mass of Ca(NO3)2?
(Atomic masses: Ca = 40.08, N = 14.01, O = 16.00 g/mol)

rationales.whyCorrect:
The subscript 2 outside the parentheses multiplies
everything inside: Ca(NO3)2 contains 1 Ca, 2 N, and 6 O. Molar mass =
40.08 + 2(14.01) + 6(16.00) = 40.08 + 28.02 + 96.00 = 164.10 g/mol.
Option B (102.09 g/mol) results from ignoring the outside subscript entirely,
treating the formula as Ca + N + 3 O = 40.08 + 14.01 + 48.00 = 102.09.
Option C (132.10 g/mol) results from misreading NO3 as NO2: 40.08 + 2(14.01)
+ 4(16.00) = 132.10. Option D (196.10 g/mol) comes from counting 8 oxygen
atoms instead of 6: 40.08 + 2(14.01) + 8(16.00) = 196.10.
rationales.eli10: Imagine a sandwich shop's combo meal: each combo has 1 drink and 1 bag of chips. If you order 3 combos, you get 3 drinks and 3 bags of chips. The subscript outside parentheses in a formula works the same way — Ca(NO3)2 means you have two whole NO3 groups. You multiply everything inside the parentheses by the outside number, just like multiplying the combo contents by the number of combos you ordered.
rationales.highYield: When a polyatomic ion appears in parentheses with an outside subscript, multiply every atom inside the parentheses by that subscript before adding masses.

questions.stem: What mass of AgCl (M = 143.32 g/mol) precipitates when 50.0 mL of 0.200 M AgNO3 is added to excess NaCl?

rationales.whyCorrect: moles AgNO3 = 0.200 M × 0.0500 L = 0.0100 mol. The reaction AgNO3 + NaCl → AgCl + NaNO3 is 1:1, so moles AgCl = 0.0100 mol. mass AgCl = 0.0100 mol × 143.32 g/mol = 1.4332 g ≈ 1.43 g. Option A results from using 25.0 mL instead of 50.0 mL. Option C doubles the moles. Option D uses the wrong molar mass or miscalculates by a factor of 5.
rationales.eli10: Solution stoichiometry is a three-step recipe. Step 1: figure out how many moles of silver nitrate you have (0.200 moles per liter × a twentieth of a liter = 0.0100 moles). Step 2: the recipe says 1 AgNO3 makes 1 AgCl. Step 3: convert 0.0100 moles to grams (× 143.32 g/mol = 1.43 g). It is like converting cups of flour to grams using the recipe ratio.
rationales.highYield: Solution stoichiometry: volume × molarity → moles A → moles B (mole ratio) → mass B.

questions.stem: According to kinetic molecular theory, the average kinetic energy of gas molecules depends only on:

rationales.whyCorrect: KMT states that KE_avg = (3/2)RT per mole, depending only on absolute temperature. All gases at the same temperature have the same average kinetic energy regardless of molar mass. Heavier gases move slower at the same temperature to maintain equal KE. Options A, B, and D are incorrect — KE is independent of these factors.
rationales.eli10: Temperature is like a universal speed setting for molecules. At 25 °C, hydrogen molecules zoom fast while CO2 molecules lumber slowly, but their average "energy of motion" is exactly the same. It is like a ping-pong ball and a bowling ball rolling at different speeds but carrying the same kinetic energy. Heat them both up, and they both get more energetic by the same amount.
rationales.highYield: KE_avg = (3/2)RT; at fixed T, all gases have equal average kinetic energy.

questions.stem: Calculate ΔH° for 2Al(s) + Fe2O3(s) → Al2O3(s) + 2Fe(s) given: ΔH_f°(Fe2O3) = -824.2 kJ/mol and ΔH_f°(Al2O3) = -1675.7 kJ/mol.

rationales.whyCorrect: ΔH° = ΣΔH_f°(products) - ΣΔH_f°(reactants) = [ΔH_f°(Al2O3) + 2×ΔH_f°(Fe)] - [2×ΔH_f°(Al) + ΔH_f°(Fe2O3)]. Elements in standard state have ΔH_f° = 0. ΔH° = [-1675.7 + 0] - [0 + (-824.2)] = -1675.7 + 824.2 = -851.5 kJ. Option A reverses the sign. Option C adds instead. Option D is the sum of both magnitudes.
rationales.eli10: Calculating reaction enthalpy from formation enthalpies is like figuring out the net cost of a transaction. Each compound has a "formation energy price tag" (ΔH_f°). Products are money received; reactants are money spent. Subtract total spent from total received. Elements cost zero because they are already in their natural form.
rationales.highYield: ΔH° = Σ nΔH_f°(products) - Σ mΔH_f°(reactants). ΔH_f° of elements in standard state = 0.

questions.stem: An electron in a 3p orbital of chlorine experiences a higher Zeff than an electron in a 3p orbital of sodium because:

options.text: Chlorine has more protons and similar shielding in the same shell

rationales.whyCorrect: Zeff = Z - S. Across Period 3, electrons are added to the same n = 3 shell, so core shielding (S) stays roughly constant. Chlorine (Z = 17) has more protons than sodium (Z = 11), giving a higher Zeff. Option A is wrong — both are in Period 3 with the same number of shells. Option C is wrong — chlorine has more electrons. Option D is incorrect.
rationales.eli10: Effective nuclear charge is like the volume of a teacher's voice heard by students in the back row, after the front-row students muffle some of it. Sodium's teacher speaks at volume 11, chlorine's teacher at volume 17. But both have the same number of front-row students (core electrons) muffling the sound. So chlorine's back-row students hear a much louder teacher — a stronger pull toward the nucleus.
rationales.highYield: Zeff increases left to right because Z increases while S stays roughly constant within a period.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes **valence bond theory**?

options.text: Electrons are completely transferred from a metal to a nonmetal, forming ions held together by electrostatic attraction.
Electrons are delocalized across the entire molecule in molecular orbitals formed from linear combinations of atomic orbitals.
A covalent bond forms when a half-filled atomic orbital from one atom overlaps with a half-filled atomic orbital from another atom, pairing the electrons with opposite spins.
Atoms share electrons until every atom achieves exactly eight valence electrons around it.

rationales.whyCorrect: Valence bond theory describes bonding as the overlap of atomic orbitals, each containing one electron, to form a shared electron pair localized between the two nuclei. Option A describes ionic bonding. Option B describes molecular orbital theory, not VB theory. Option D describes the octet rule, which is a guideline but not a bonding theory.
rationales.eli10: Valence bond theory is like two neighbors each holding one end of the same rope. Each neighbor brings one hand (half-filled orbital), and when their hands overlap, they both grip the rope (shared electron pair). The bond lives right in the space where the hands meet — it is localized between them. Neither neighbor lets go; the shared grip is what keeps them connected.
rationales.highYield: Valence bond theory = localized orbital overlap + electron pairing. Each bond is a shared electron pair between two atoms.

questions.stem: How does **molecular orbital theory** differ from valence bond theory?

options.text: MO theory applies only to ionic compounds, while VB theory applies only to covalent compounds.
MO theory treats each bond as a localized electron pair between two specific atoms.
MO theory describes electrons in orbitals that extend over the entire molecule rather than being localized between pairs of atoms.
MO theory ignores atomic orbitals entirely and builds molecular orbitals from scratch.

rationales.whyCorrect: MO theory treats molecular orbitals as linear combinations of atomic orbitals (LCAO), producing orbitals that are delocalized across the whole molecule. This explains phenomena VB theory cannot, such as paramagnetism of O2. Option A is false — both theories apply to covalent compounds. Option B describes VB theory, not MO theory. Option D is wrong — MO theory builds molecular orbitals from atomic orbitals via LCAO.
rationales.eli10: VB theory is like describing a house room by room — each bond is its own separate room. MO theory is like looking at the house from above with a thermal camera — you see heat (electrons) spread across the whole house, not just in separate rooms. This big-picture view lets MO theory explain things VB theory misses, like why oxygen molecules are attracted to a magnet even though all their electrons look paired on paper.
rationales.highYield: VB = electrons localized between atom pairs. MO = electrons delocalized in molecular orbitals spanning the whole molecule.

questions.stem: According to valence bond theory, a carbon atom with **sp^2 hybridization** has:

options.text: Three sp^2 hybrid orbitals arranged in a trigonal planar geometry (120° apart) plus one unhybridized p orbital perpendicular to the plane.
Four equivalent sp^3 hybrid orbitals arranged in a tetrahedral geometry (109.5° apart).
Two sp hybrid orbitals arranged linearly (180° apart) plus two unhybridized p orbitals.
Five sp^3d hybrid orbitals arranged in a trigonal bipyramidal geometry.

rationales.whyCorrect: sp^2 hybridization mixes one s orbital with two p orbitals, producing three equivalent hybrid orbitals at 120° angles (trigonal planar). The remaining unhybridized p orbital is perpendicular to this plane and participates in pi bonding. Option B describes sp^3 hybridization. Option C describes sp hybridization. Option D describes sp^3d hybridization, which carbon never uses.
rationales.eli10: Hybridization is like blending paint colors. sp^2 means you mix one bucket of s paint with two buckets of p paint, producing three identical buckets of sp^2-colored paint. These three buckets spread out equally, like three people trying to stand as far apart as possible on a flat surface — they form a triangle (120° apart). The leftover p orbital that did not get mixed sits perpendicular, like a flagpole sticking straight out of the triangle, ready to form a pi bond.
rationales.highYield: sp = linear (180°), sp^2 = trigonal planar (120°), sp^3 = tetrahedral (109.5°). Count hybrid orbitals = number of electron domains.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: In a sealed hypothetical reaction vessel, 4 g of hydrogen gas reacts completely with 32 g of oxygen gas to form water as the only product. Which value states the mass of water produced, and which principle requires it?

options.text: 34 g, because a small amount of mass is converted to the heat released
32 g, because the heavier reactant determines the mass of the product
18 g, because one mole of water has a mass of 18 g
36 g, because mass is conserved in a chemical reaction

rationales.whyCorrect: The law of conservation of mass states that atoms are neither created nor destroyed in a chemical change, so in a closed system the total mass of products equals the total mass of reactants. Here 4 g of H2 (2 mol) and 32 g of O2 (1 mol) match the 2:1 ratio of 2 H2 + O2 to 2 H2O exactly, so both are fully consumed and all 36 g of matter appears as water. The energy released is real but the associated mass change is far too small to measure chemically, which is why chemical equations are balanced on an atom-for-atom basis.
rationales.eli10: A chemical reaction rearranges atoms; it never deletes them or invents new ones. Take apart a 36-piece structure and rebuild it into a different shape inside a sealed box, and the box still holds 36 pieces. So 4 g in plus 32 g in must come out as 36 g of water. Reactions release energy, but that does not make measurable matter disappear.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which set of coefficients, written in the order N2, H2, NH3, balances the equation N2 + H2 -> NH3 using the smallest whole numbers?

rationales.whyCorrect: With 1, 3, 2 the left side has 2 N and 6 H and the right side has 2 N and 6 H, so every element balances with the smallest possible whole numbers. Each other set fails an atom count: 1, 2, 2 gives 4 H on the left against 6 H on the right; 2, 3, 2 gives 4 N on the left against 2 N on the right; 1, 3, 3 gives 2 N on the left against 3 N on the right. Balancing is done only by adjusting coefficients, because changing a subscript would change the identity of a substance.
rationales.eli10: Count atoms on each side and adjust only the numbers written in front. One N2 supplies 2 nitrogen atoms, and each NH3 uses 1 nitrogen, so 2 NH3 can be built. Those 2 NH3 need 6 hydrogen atoms, and hydrogen arrives as H2 pairs, so 3 H2 are required. Final tally: 2 N and 6 H on both sides.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which equation is an example of a decomposition reaction?

rationales.whyCorrect: Decomposition follows the pattern AB -> A + B: a single reactant breaks apart into two or more simpler substances. Hydrogen peroxide breaking down into water and oxygen gas is exactly that pattern. The distractors are a single-replacement reaction (zinc displacing hydrogen from the acid), a combination or synthesis reaction (two elements forming one compound), and a double-replacement precipitation reaction.
rationales.eli10: Classify by counting what starts and what ends. Decomposition has exactly one starting substance that comes apart into several products. Synthesis is the reverse: several reactants combine into one product. Replacement reactions start with two substances that swap partners. Only the peroxide equation begins with a single compound, so only it is decomposition.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A student tries to "balance" H2 + O2 -> H2O by rewriting the product formula as H2O2. What is wrong with this approach?

options.text: The mass on each side changes, but the identity of the product stays the same
The equation stays chemically valid because a subscript was changed, not a coefficient
The equation is acceptable because subscripts and coefficients both scale the product amount
The equation no longer describes water; it describes hydrogen peroxide, a different compound

rationales.whyCorrect: Subscripts specify the fixed composition of a compound, so changing one produces a different substance rather than a different quantity of the same substance. H2O and H2O2 differ by one oxygen atom per molecule and have entirely different chemical properties: water is stable and drinkable, hydrogen peroxide is a reactive oxidizer that decomposes readily. Balancing is legitimate only when correct formulas are held fixed and coefficients in front of them are adjusted.
rationales.eli10: A formula is the substance's identity; a coefficient is how many units of it are present. If a reaction needs more water, you write a larger number in front of H2O. Editing the subscript instead changes what the substance is, the way changing letters inside a word changes the word rather than giving you two copies of it.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A hypothetical laboratory burner combusts propane completely: C3H8 + 5 O2 -> 3 CO2 + 4 H2O. How many moles of O2 are consumed when 2 mol of propane burns completely?

options.text: 2.5 mol, because the 2 mol of propane is divided by the 5:1 ratio
10 mol, because the 5:1 mole ratio is applied to 2 mol of propane
5 mol, because the coefficient of O2 in the balanced equation is 5
8 mol, because the water coefficient of 4 is scaled to the 2 mol of propane

rationales.whyCorrect: Coefficients in a balanced equation express mole ratios, and this equation requires 5 mol O2 per 1 mol C3H8. Multiplying that ratio by 2 mol of propane gives 2 x 5 = 10 mol O2. Reading a coefficient as a fixed absolute amount, inverting the ratio, or picking the coefficient of the wrong species are the three common errors represented by the distractors.
rationales.eli10: Treat the balanced equation as a ratio, not a fixed quantity. It says every 1 propane pairs with 5 oxygen molecules. Doubling the propane doubles everything tied to it, so 2 propane pairs with 10 oxygen. The key move is to set up the ratio as 5 mol O2 per 1 mol C3H8 and multiply, so the propane units cancel and moles of O2 remain.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: In a teaching demonstration, hydrochloric acid is neutralized by calcium hydroxide: 2 HCl + Ca(OH)2 -> CaCl2 + 2 H2O. How many moles of Ca(OH)2 are required to neutralize 0.4 mol of HCl completely?

options.text: 0.2 mol, because each mole of Ca(OH)2 supplies two moles of hydroxide
0.4 mol, because an acid and a base always neutralize in a 1:1 ratio
0.1 mol, because each of the two hydroxide ions neutralizes two moles of acid
0.8 mol, because each mole of HCl requires two moles of the base

rationales.whyCorrect: The balanced equation sets a 2:1 mole ratio of HCl to Ca(OH)2, so 0.4 mol HCl requires 0.4 / 2 = 0.2 mol of the base. Each formula unit of Ca(OH)2 releases two hydroxide ions, so one mole of it neutralizes two moles of a monoprotic acid such as HCl. Assuming every acid-base pairing is 1:1 is a frequent misconception that produces a twofold error in the amount of base.
rationales.eli10: Neutralization pairs one H+ with one OH-. HCl delivers one H+ per formula unit, while Ca(OH)2 delivers two OH- per formula unit. So each unit of base can handle two units of this acid, and you need only half as many moles of base as acid: 0.4 divided by 2 is 0.2 mol.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which statement about the complete ionic and net ionic equations for AgNO3(aq) + NaCl(aq) -> AgCl(s) + NaNO3(aq) is accurate?

options.text: The net ionic equation lists all four ions, since each of them is dissolved in water
The net ionic equation drops Ag+ and Cl-, since ions that form a solid are not written
The net ionic equation drops the spectator ions Na+ and NO3-, leaving Ag+ + Cl- -> AgCl(s)
The complete ionic equation writes AgCl as separate Ag+ and Cl- ions in solution

rationales.whyCorrect: In the complete ionic equation, soluble strong electrolytes are written as dissociated ions while the insoluble product AgCl is written as an intact solid. Na+ and NO3- appear unchanged on both sides, so they are spectator ions and cancel, leaving Ag+(aq) + Cl-(aq) -> AgCl(s). The net ionic equation isolates the chemical change that actually occurs, which is why it is the standard representation for precipitation and neutralization reactions.
rationales.eli10: Write out every dissolved ion first, but keep the insoluble solid together because it is not dissociated. Then cross off any ion that appears identically on both sides; it entered and left unchanged, so it did nothing. Here Na+ and NO3- cancel, and what survives is the silver ion joining the chloride ion to form solid AgCl.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A sealed hypothetical vessel is charged with 4 mol H2 and 3 mol O2, which react by 2 H2 + O2 -> 2 H2O. Which outcome is expected once the reaction goes to completion?

options.text: 3 mol of water forms, with 1 mol of H2 left unreacted
6 mol of water forms, with all 3 mol of O2 consumed
4 mol of water forms, with 1 mol of O2 left unreacted
7 mol of water forms, with both gases fully consumed

rationales.whyCorrect: Divide each amount by its coefficient: H2 gives 4 / 2 = 2 reaction units, O2 gives 3 / 1 = 3, so H2 is limiting. The 4 mol of H2 produces 4 mol of H2O and consumes only 2 mol of O2, leaving 1 mol of O2 in excess. The limiting reactant is set by stoichiometric demand, not by which reactant simply has the smaller number of moles or the smaller coefficient.
rationales.eli10: Ask how many complete reactions each reactant could support. Hydrogen is used two at a time, so 4 mol of H2 supports 2 rounds. Oxygen is used one at a time, so 3 mol of O2 supports 3 rounds. Only 2 rounds can actually run, and each round makes 2 water, giving 4 mol of water. Those 2 rounds use 2 mol of O2, so 1 mol of O2 sits unused.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: In a hypothetical student synthesis, the calculated theoretical yield of a salt is 25 g and the mass actually isolated after purification is 20 g. What is the percent yield of the reaction?

options.text: 125%, found by dividing the theoretical yield by the actual yield
80%, found by dividing the actual yield by the theoretical yield
20%, because the isolated mass in grams is reported directly as the percentage
0.8%, found from the ratio of actual to theoretical without converting to a percentage

rationales.whyCorrect: Percent yield = (actual yield / theoretical yield) x 100 = (20 / 25) x 100 = 80%. Theoretical yield comes from the balanced equation applied to the limiting reactant; actual yield is what is physically recovered, and it is normally lower because of side reactions, incomplete reaction, and losses during transfer and filtration. A reported yield above 100% almost always signals an impure or incompletely dried product rather than extra material.
rationales.eli10: Percent yield compares what you got with what the stoichiometry promised. You were promised 25 g and recovered 20 g, so you kept 20 out of every 25, which is 4 out of every 5, or 80 out of 100. Two habits prevent errors here: put the actual amount on top, and remember to multiply the ratio by 100.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: In a hypothetical furnace demonstration, calcium carbonate decomposes completely: CaCO3(s) -> CaO(s) + CO2(g). Using 44 g/mol as the molar mass of CO2, what mass of CO2 is released when 2 mol of CaCO3 decomposes?

options.text: 22 g, obtained by dividing the 44 g/mol molar mass between the 2 mol of CaCO3
200 g, because the 100 g/mol molar mass of CaCO3 is applied to the 2 mol
44 g, because one mole of CO2 leaves the solid no matter how large the sample is
88 g, because 2 mol of CO2 forms and each mole has a mass of 44 g

rationales.whyCorrect: The balanced equation has a 1:1 mole ratio of CaCO3 to CO2, so 2 mol of carbonate releases 2 mol of CO2. Converting moles to mass with the molar mass of the gas gives 2 mol x 44 g/mol = 88 g. The two-step pattern of moles of reactant, then mole ratio, then molar mass of the requested substance is the standard route for every mass-based stoichiometry calculation, and the molar mass used must belong to the substance being asked about.
rationales.eli10: Work in two steps. First use the equation's ratio: one CaCO3 releases one CO2, so 2 mol in means 2 mol of gas out. Then convert moles of gas to grams using the molar mass of that gas: 2 x 44 = 88 g. The common trap is grabbing the molar mass of the starting solid instead of the substance the question asks for.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Butane undergoes complete combustion according to the unbalanced equation C4H10 + O2 -> CO2 + H2O. When the equation is balanced with the smallest possible whole-number coefficients, what is the sum of all four coefficients?

rationales.whyCorrect: Balancing carbon and hydrogen first gives C4H10 + 13/2 O2 -> 4 CO2 + 5 H2O, and multiplying every coefficient by 2 clears the fraction to give 2 C4H10 + 13 O2 -> 8 CO2 + 10 H2O, so the coefficients sum to 2 + 13 + 8 + 10 = 33. The atom inventory confirms 8 C, 20 H, and 26 O on each side, since 13 x 2 = 26 and (8 x 2) + 10 = 26. The sums 24 and 29 arise from doubling only some of the coefficients after clearing the fraction (24 = 2 + 13 + 4 + 5 and 29 = 2 + 13 + 4 + 10), while 31 is simply a nearby total that no correct balancing produces.
rationales.eli10: Balance carbon and hydrogen first because each appears in only one product, and leave oxygen for last because it appears in two. That gives 4 CO2 and 5 H2O, which need 13 oxygen atoms, or 6.5 O2 molecules. Since half a molecule is not allowed, multiply every coefficient in the equation by 2, exactly as you would double a whole recipe rather than one ingredient. The result is 2, 13, 8, 10, which adds to 33.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Ammonia is produced by N2 + 3 H2 -> 2 NH3. A sealed hypothetical reactor is charged with 2 mol N2 and 3 mol H2. Using 17 g/mol as the molar mass of NH3, what is the theoretical yield of ammonia?

options.text: 51 g, because each mole of H2 charged yields one mole of NH3
68 g, because N2 is limiting and yields 4 mol of NH3
34 g, because H2 is limiting and yields 2 mol of NH3
85 g, because all 5 mol of reactant charged is converted to product

rationales.whyCorrect: Divide each amount by its coefficient: N2 gives 2 / 1 = 2 reaction units while H2 gives 3 / 3 = 1, so hydrogen is the limiting reactant and 1 mol of N2 remains in excess. Applying the 3:2 ratio, 3 mol of H2 produces 2 mol of NH3, and 2 mol x 17 g/mol = 34 g. Comparing raw mole counts would point to N2 as limiting because only 2 mol were charged, which is exactly the error behind choice B; only the moles-divided-by-coefficient comparison correctly identifies H2 as the limiting reactant.
rationales.eli10: Each complete reaction consumes 1 N2 and 3 H2. With 3 mol of H2 you can run exactly one such reaction, and with 2 mol of N2 you could run two, so hydrogen runs out first and 1 mol of nitrogen is left over. That single reaction produces 2 mol of NH3, and at 17 g per mole that is 34 g. Notice that nitrogen is the one you have less of by simple count, yet hydrogen is what runs out, so always divide each amount by its coefficient before deciding which reactant limits the yield.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A car travels at 65.0 miles per hour. Convert this speed to meters per second. (1 mile = 1609 m, 1 hour = 3600 s)

rationales.whyCorrect: Using dimensional analysis: 65.0 mi/hr × (1609 m / 1 mi) × (1 hr / 3600 s) = (65.0 × 1609) / 3600 = 104585 / 3600 = 29.05 m/s. With three significant figures (limited by 65.0), the answer is 29.1 m/s. Option B results from inverting the time conversion (multiplying by 3600 instead of dividing). Option C converts miles to meters but forgets to convert hours to seconds, reporting meters per hour mislabeled as meters per second. Option D uses 1000 m per mile instead of 1609 m.
rationales.eli10: Converting units is like trading currency. You have 65 miles in your pocket, and each mile is worth 1609 meters — so you now have a lot of meters. But your speed was per hour, and you need it per second, so you divide by 3600 (the number of seconds in an hour). The result: about 29 meters every second, which makes sense — a car at highway speed covers roughly the length of a basketball court each second.
rationales.highYield: In dimensional analysis, write each conversion factor as a fraction so units cancel diagonally; multiply all numerators and divide by all denominators.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: John Dalton's original atomic theory contained several postulates. Which one has been modified by the discovery of isotopes?

options.text: Atoms of different elements have different masses.
Atoms combine in simple whole-number ratios to form compounds.
All atoms of the same element are identical in mass and properties.
Chemical reactions rearrange atoms but do not create or destroy them.

rationales.whyCorrect: Dalton believed all atoms of a given element were identical in every way, including mass. The discovery of isotopes — atoms of the same element that differ in neutron count and therefore mass — showed that atoms of the same element can have different masses while sharing the same chemical properties. Option A remains correct: different elements have different numbers of protons and therefore different properties. Option B is still valid for stoichiometric compounds. Option D is the law of conservation of mass, which still holds.
rationales.eli10: Dalton thought all carbon atoms were like identical marbles from the same factory — every one exactly the same. But we now know carbon atoms come in slightly different weights, like different sizes of the same brand of basketball. Carbon-12, carbon-13, and carbon-14 are all still carbon and behave the same chemically, but their masses are different because they have different numbers of neutrons.
rationales.highYield: Dalton's theory had to be revised because isotopes of the same element have different masses, even though they share the same number of protons.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which element has the largest atomic radius?

rationales.whyCorrect: Atomic radius increases down a group (added electron shells) and decreases across a period (higher Zeff pulls electrons inward). Potassium is in Period 4, Group 1, at the far left and fairly low on the table. Fluorine (Period 2) and chlorine (Period 3) are both halogens, small because of high Zeff. Bromine (Period 4, Group 17) is farther right than potassium and has a much higher Zeff, so it is smaller. Among the choices, potassium — a Period 4 alkali metal — is the largest.
rationales.eli10: Think of the periodic table like a staircase: atoms on the bottom-left step are big and floppy, while atoms on the top-right step are small and tight. Going down adds more floors to the atom (more shells), which makes it bigger. Going right adds more protons pulling the same number of shells inward, which makes it smaller. Potassium sits low and left — it has four floors but only one strong puller, so it spreads out wide.
rationales.highYield: Atomic radius decreases left to right across a period and increases top to bottom down a group. The largest atoms are in the bottom-left corner of the periodic table.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which element requires the most energy to remove one electron from a neutral gaseous atom?

rationales.whyCorrect: Ionization energy increases across a period (higher Zeff) and decreases down a group (more shielding, larger radius). Helium is in Period 1 with the smallest atomic radius among the choices and only one shell. Its two electrons experience the full +2 nuclear charge with almost no shielding, making them extremely hard to remove. Neon (Period 2), argon (Period 3), and krypton (Period 4) are all noble gases with full valence shells, but each is progressively larger with more inner-shell shielding, so their ionization energies decrease down the group. Helium has the highest first ionization energy of any element.
rationales.eli10: Picture the nucleus as a parent holding their child's hand. In helium, there are only two electrons very close to a +2 nucleus — the parent has a tight grip on both kids. In krypton, there are 36 electrons spread across four shells, so the outermost electrons are far away, with many other kids blocking the parent's reach. The farther away and the more shielded the electron, the easier it is to pull free — so helium holds on tightest.
rationales.highYield: Ionization energy follows the same direction as Zeff: increases across a period, decreases down a group. Helium has the highest first ionization energy of all elements.

subjectWideQuestions.stem:
A compound is found to contain 85.63% carbon and 14.37% hydrogen by mass.
What is its empirical formula? (Atomic masses: C = 12.01 g/mol, H = 1.008 g/mol)

rationales.whyCorrect:
Assume a 100.00 g sample: 85.63 g C and 14.37 g H.
Convert to moles: C = 85.63 g / 12.01 g/mol = 7.130 mol;
H = 14.37 g / 1.008 g/mol = 14.26 mol. Divide both by the smaller value
(7.130 mol): C = 7.130 / 7.130 = 1.00; H = 14.26 / 7.130 = 2.00.
The 1:2 mole ratio gives the empirical formula CH2. Option A (CH) results
from mistakenly taking the raw mole counts as the ratio without dividing.
Option B (CH3) arises from misreading the H percentage or miscalculating
the division step. Option D (C2H4) is a molecular formula, not the
simplest ratio — the student skipped the division step entirely.
rationales.eli10: A recipe for lemonade says "2 cups water for every 1 cup lemon juice." That ratio works whether you are making one pitcher or a whole bathtub. The empirical formula is that ratio — just the simplest recipe for the molecule, not the full ingredient list for one batch. Two totally different cakes can share the same flour-to-sugar ratio, just like two different compounds can share the same empirical formula.
rationales.highYield: Empirical formula is the simplest whole-number ratio of atoms; divide each element's moles by the smallest mole value to find it, then multiply all ratios by a small integer if any is not within 0.1 of a whole number.

subjectWideQuestions.stem:
A reaction has a theoretical yield of 45.0 g of product. The actual mass of
product recovered after the experiment is 36.0 g. What is the percent yield?

rationales.whyCorrect:
Percent yield = (actual yield / theoretical yield) × 100%
= (36.0 g / 45.0 g) × 100% = 80.0%. Option B (20.0%) is the percent lost, not
the percent recovered: (45.0 - 36.0) / 45.0 × 100% = 20.0%. Option C (44.4%)
results from dividing the actual yield by the sum of actual and theoretical
yields: 36.0 / (36.0 + 45.0) × 100% = 44.4%. Option D (125%) inverts the ratio:
45.0 / 36.0 × 100% = 125%.
rationales.eli10: You bake batter for 12 muffins — that is your theoretical yield. Some batter sticks to the bowl, and two muffins crumble coming out of the tin, so you end up with 9 perfect muffins. Your percent yield is (9 / 12) × 100% = 75%. The missing muffins represent product lost to the equipment and handling, exactly like product stuck to filter paper in a chemistry lab. If you somehow ended up with 13 muffins, you would know something else got mixed in — that is what a percent yield above 100% means.
rationales.highYield: Percent yield = (actual yield / theoretical yield) × 100%; values above 100% indicate contamination or measurement error, not extra product.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: What is the molarity of a solution prepared by dissolving 5.85 g of NaCl (M = 58.44 g/mol) in enough water to make 250.0 mL of solution?

rationales.whyCorrect: moles NaCl = 5.85 g / 58.44 g/mol = 0.1001 mol. Molarity = moles / liters = 0.1001 mol / 0.2500 L = 0.4004 M ≈ 0.400 M. Option A results from dividing by the wrong volume (1.00 L instead of 0.250 L). Option B comes from using half the correct molar mass. Option D comes from using 125 mL instead of 250 mL.
rationales.eli10: Molarity is like making lemonade from powder. You measure the powder first (5.85 g of salt is about a teaspoon), dissolve it, then add water until the pitcher reads exactly 250 mL. If you just add 250 mL of water to the powder without measuring the final volume, the actual volume would be slightly more and the lemonade would be too weak.
rationales.highYield: M = mol solute / L solution; final volume is the total solution volume, not the volume of solvent added.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: What volume of 6.00 M HCl is required to prepare 500.0 mL of 0.300 M HCl?

rationales.whyCorrect: Using M1V1 = M2V2: (6.00 M)(V1) = (0.300 M)(500.0 mL). V1 = (0.300 × 500.0) / 6.00 = 150.0 / 6.00 = 25.0 mL. Option A results from reversing the M1 and M2 values. Option C comes from using 1000 mL instead of 500 mL. Option D results from an incorrect ratio (6.00/0.300 = 20, then 500/20 = 25... no, that is correct — option D is a different error, perhaps using V2 directly).
rationales.eli10: Dilution is like making weak coffee from strong concentrate. If the concentrate is 20 times stronger than you want (6.00 M vs 0.300 M), you only need 1/20th of your final cup volume as concentrate. 500 mL divided by 20 equals 25 mL of concentrate — the rest is water. The total moles of HCl never change; they are just spread through more water.
rationales.highYield: M1V1 = M2V2 works because moles are conserved during dilution; any volume units are fine as long as both sides match.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: If 10.0 mL of a stock solution is diluted to a final volume of 250.0 mL, by what factor is the concentration reduced?

rationales.whyCorrect: The dilution factor is V_final / V_initial = 250.0 mL / 10.0 mL = 25. The concentration after dilution is 1/25 of the original. Option A confuses the initial volume with the factor. Option C doubles the correct factor. Option D uses the final volume directly.
rationales.eli10: Dilution factor is like stretching a rubber band. You start with a short 10 mL piece and stretch it to 250 mL — it is now 25 times longer but 25 times thinner. The total amount of "rubber" (moles) stays the same, but it is spread over 25 times more space, so the concentration drops to 1/25th of the original.
rationales.highYield: Dilution factor = V_final / V_initial. Concentration decreases by the same factor.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which gas effuses faster, and by what factor: He (4.00 g/mol) or O2 (32.00 g/mol)?

rationales.whyCorrect: Graham's law: rate_He / rate_O2 = sqrt(M_O2 / M_He) = sqrt(32.00 / 4.00) = sqrt(8.00) = 2.828. Helium is lighter and effuses faster. Option A reverses the ratio. Option C incorrectly uses the ratio directly without the square root. Option D uses the direct ratio and the wrong direction.
rationales.eli10: Effusion is like two crowds escaping through a narrow doorway — a crowd of lightweight children escapes faster than a crowd of heavy adults. Helium atoms weigh only 4 units each, oxygen molecules weigh 32 — eight times heavier. But the speed depends on the square root of the weight ratio, so helium escapes about 2.83 times faster, not 8 times.
rationales.highYield: rate_A / rate_B = sqrt(M_B / M_A). Lighter gases effuse faster.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A gas occupies 5.00 L at 2.00 atm. If the temperature and amount remain constant, what volume does it occupy at 5.00 atm?

rationales.whyCorrect: Boyle's law: P1V1 = P2V2. V2 = P1V1/P2 = (2.00 atm × 5.00 L) / 5.00 atm = 10.0/5.00 = 2.00 L. Option A incorrectly divides 5 by 5. Option C multiplies instead of solving for V2. Option D uses an incorrect formula.
rationales.eli10: Boyle's law is like squeezing a balloon. Push harder (increase pressure from 2 to 5 atm — 2.5 times more), and the balloon shrinks. The volume goes from 5.00 L down to 2.00 L. Double the pressure, half the volume — they are perfectly balanced like a seesaw.
rationales.highYield: At constant T and n, P1V1 = P2V2. Pressure and volume are inversely proportional.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: At constant temperature and pressure, 2.0 L of H2 gas contains 0.080 mol. How many moles are in 5.0 L of H2 at the same T and P?

rationales.whyCorrect: Avogadro's law: V1/n1 = V2/n2. n2 = n1 × V2/V1 = 0.080 mol × (5.0 L / 2.0 L) = 0.080 × 2.5 = 0.20 mol. Option A inverts the volume ratio. Option B ignores the volume change. Option D doubles the correct answer.
rationales.eli10: Avogadro's law is like a parking lot — double the number of cars and you need double the parking spaces. If 2.0 liters holds 0.080 moles of gas, then 5.0 liters (2.5 times bigger) holds 2.5 times more moles — 0.20 moles. Same parking rules apply to any gas.
rationales.highYield: At constant T and P, V ∝ n. Equal volumes contain equal numbers of molecules.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A gas is collected over water at 25 °C. The total pressure is 755 torr. If the vapor pressure of water at 25 °C is 23.8 torr, what is the partial pressure of the dry gas?

rationales.whyCorrect: P_dry_gas = P_total - P_H2O = 755 torr - 23.8 torr = 731.2 torr ≈ 731 torr. Water vapor contributes to the total pressure and must be subtracted. Option A is the water vapor pressure alone. Option C is the total pressure. Option D incorrectly adds the pressures.
rationales.eli10: Collecting gas over water is like measuring the crowd noise at a concert but remembering to subtract the hum of the air conditioner. The total pressure (755 torr) includes both the gas you collected and water vapor that evaporated into the container (23.8 torr). Subtract the water vapor to find how much pressure belongs to your gas alone — 731 torr.
rationales.highYield: When collecting gas over water: P_dry_gas = P_total - P_H2O(vapor).

subjectWideQuestions.stem: In the van der Waals equation, the parameter "a" corrects for:

options.text: The finite volume of gas particles
The kinetic energy of the particles
The number of moles of gas

rationales.whyCorrect: The van der Waals term n^2·a/V^2 corrects for attractive forces between gas molecules, which reduce the effective pressure. The parameter b corrects for particle volume. Option A describes parameter b. Options C and D are not van der Waals corrections.
rationales.eli10: The van der Waals "a" is like a stickiness factor. Real gas molecules are slightly sticky — they attract each other. When they stick a bit, they hit the walls less hard, so the measured pressure is lower than ideal. The "a" correction adds back the missing pressure from stickiness. The "b" correction is for the space the molecules themselves occupy — they are not true points.
rationales.highYield: van der Waals: (P + n^2·a/V^2)(V - n·b) = nRT. a = attraction correction; b = volume correction.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Given: C(s) + O2(g) → CO2(g), ΔH = -393.5 kJ. 2CO(g) + O2(g) → 2CO2(g), ΔH = -566.0 kJ. What is ΔH for C(s) + 1/2 O2(g) → CO(g)?

rationales.whyCorrect: Target = C + 1/2 O2 → CO. Manipulate given: (1) C + O2 → CO2, ΔH = -393.5. (2) Reverse and halve: CO2 → CO + 1/2 O2, ΔH = +566.0/2 = +283.0 (reversed, sign flips). Add: C + O2 + CO2 → CO2 + CO + 1/2 O2. Cancel CO2 and 1/2 O2. ΔH = -393.5 + 283.0 = -110.5 kJ. Option A has wrong sign. Option C drops the factor of 1/2. Option D adds instead of subtracting.
rationales.eli10: Hess's law is like calculating total elevation change on a hike. You do not need to walk the whole trail at once — you can add up the climbs and descents of each segment. If you go up 393 feet then down 283 feet, you end up 110 feet lower than where you started. The path does not matter; only the start and end points do. Enthalpy is the same way — it is a state function.
rationales.highYield: Hess's law: add known ΔH values algebraically. Reverse a reaction → flip sign. Multiply → multiply ΔH.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which of the following correctly describes the trend in atomic radius across Period 3 (Na to Ar)?

options.text: Radius increases because more protons are added
Radius decreases because effective nuclear charge increases
Radius stays constant because electrons are in the same shell
Radius decreases because more neutrons are added

rationales.whyCorrect: Across Period 3, electrons are added to the same n = 3 shell, but protons are added to the nucleus. Zeff increases because core shielding stays roughly constant while nuclear charge increases, pulling valence electrons closer. Option A incorrectly predicts increase. Option C ignores the effect of increasing Zeff. Option D incorrectly attributes the trend to neutrons.
rationales.eli10: Moving across a period is like the teacher (nucleus) getting louder while all students (electrons) stay in the same classroom. The louder teacher pulls everyone in closer, so the radius shrinks.
