Going down a group is like moving to a bigger classroom with more rows — even with a loud teacher, the back-row students sit farther away.
rationales.highYield: Atomic radius decreases left to right (increasing Zeff) and increases top to bottom (adding new shells).

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which element has the highest first ionization energy?

rationales.whyCorrect: First ionization energy generally increases left to right across a period due to increasing Zeff. Argon, being a noble gas with a filled octet (stable electron configuration), has the highest ionization energy in Period 3. Na has the lowest (one loosely held 3s electron). Mg and Al are intermediate. The noble gas stability makes Ar exceptionally hard to ionize.
rationales.eli10: Ionization energy is like how hard you must pull to snatch an electron away. Argon holds its electrons in a perfectly complete, comfortable set of eight — it fights hard to keep them. Sodium has one lonely electron that it barely holds onto — a gentle tug and it lets go. Noble gases are the stingiest with electrons; alkali metals are the most generous.
rationales.highYield: Ionization energy increases left to right (higher Zeff) and decreases top to bottom. Noble gases have the highest IE in each period.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: What is the formal charge on nitrogen in the ammonium ion NH4+?

rationales.whyCorrect: Formal charge = valence - nonbonding - (1/2 bonding). N has 5 valence electrons. In NH4+, N has 0 nonbonding electrons and 8 bonding electrons (4 N-H bonds). FC = 5 - 0 - (8/2) = 5 - 4 = +1. The overall ion charge is +1, matching the sum of formal charges. Option A would use 10 bonding electrons. Option B assumes N is neutral. Option D uses incorrect arithmetic.
rationales.eli10: Formal charge is like splitting a restaurant bill. Nitrogen brought 5 dollars (valence electrons) to the table. It owns none of the electrons entirely (no lone pairs) and shares equally in all four bonds, so it claims 4 dollars worth (half of 8 bonding electrons). 5 minus 4 equals +1 — nitrogen paid more than its share, so it has a positive formal charge.
rationales.highYield: FC = valence e- - nonbonding e- - (1/2 bonding e-). Sum of FCs = overall ion charge.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which element is the most electronegative?

rationales.whyCorrect: Electronegativity increases left to right and decreases top to bottom, making fluorine (top-right corner, excluding noble gases) the most electronegative element at 4.0 on the Pauling scale. Oxygen (3.5) and chlorine (3.0) are highly electronegative but not the maximum. Nitrogen (3.0) is less electronegative than oxygen.
rationales.eli10: Electronegativity is like how aggressively an atom hogs shared electrons. Fluorine is the greediest electron-hog in chemistry — when it bonds with anything, it pulls the electrons so hard toward itself that the bond becomes highly polar. It sits in the top-right corner of the periodic table, the prime real estate for electron-grabbing power.
rationales.highYield: Electronegativity: F (4.0) > O (3.5) > Cl, N (3.0). Trend: increases up and to the right on the periodic table.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which molecule or ion exhibits resonance?

rationales.whyCorrect: The nitrate ion NO3^- has three equivalent resonance structures — the double bond can be placed between N and any of the three O atoms. The true structure is a resonance hybrid with delocalized electrons. CH4, H2O, and NH3 have only one valid Lewis structure each with no electron delocalization.
rationales.eli10: Resonance is like describing a rhinoceros to someone who only knows horses and unicorns. You draw three pictures, each with the horn on a different oxygen. The real animal is an average of all three — the electrons are smeared out over all the oxygens. The molecule does not switch between forms; it is always the blend. That is why all three N-O bonds in nitrate are identical in length.
rationales.highYield: Resonance occurs when multiple valid Lewis structures differ only in electron placement. Delocalized electrons lower overall energy.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which molecule has an incomplete octet around the central atom?

rationales.whyCorrect: Boron in BF3 has only 6 valence electrons (3 B-F bonds × 2 e- each), not 8. Boron is in Group 13 with 3 valence electrons and forms only 3 bonds, leaving an incomplete octet. CH4 (C has 8), NH3 (N has 8), and H2O (O has 8) all follow the octet rule.
rationales.eli10: The octet rule is like a rule that everyone needs 8 guests at a dinner party. Boron is a rebel — it only has 3 valence electrons to share and makes only 3 bonds, so it ends up with 6 guests. It is perfectly happy with 6 because it sits in Group 13. Boron is small and does not mind the smaller crowd — it is electron-deficient but stable.
rationales.highYield: Common octet exceptions: Be (4 e-), B (6 e-), elements period 3+ (expanded octet), odd-electron radicals.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which molecule has polar bonds but is nonpolar overall?

rationales.whyCorrect: CCl4 has four polar C-Cl bonds, but the molecule is tetrahedral and perfectly symmetric. Each C-Cl bond dipole points from the central carbon to a chlorine at a corner of the tetrahedron, and the four equal dipoles cancel vectorially, producing a net dipole moment of zero. H2O (bent) and NH3 (trigonal pyramidal) are asymmetric and their bond dipoles do not cancel — both are polar. CHCl3 has three C-Cl bonds and one C-H bond; the asymmetry makes it polar.
rationales.eli10: Imagine four equally strong people pulling on ropes tied to a central ring, each pulling toward a different corner of a square-based pyramid. Because they all pull equally in perfectly symmetric directions, the ring does not move — the pulls cancel out. That is CCl4. In water, the two people pulling are standing at an angle, so the ring moves — the pulls add up to a net tug. Symmetry is everything when deciding if a molecule is polar.
rationales.highYield: A molecule can have polar bonds but be nonpolar overall if its geometry is symmetric and bond dipoles cancel. CCl4, CO2, and BF3 are classic nonpolar molecules with polar bonds.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: In the reaction Zn(s) + Cu2+(aq) → Zn2+(aq) + Cu(s), which species is reduced?

rationales.whyCorrect: Reduction is gain of electrons (oxidation number decreases). Cu2+ (+2) → Cu (0): gains 2 electrons, reduced. Zn (0) → Zn2+ (+2): loses 2 electrons, oxidized. Zn is the reducing agent. Cu2+ is the oxidizing agent. OIL RIG: Oxidation Is Loss, Reduction Is Gain.
rationales.eli10: Redox is like a basketball game with two teams playing electron-ball. Zinc loses two electrons (gets oxidized — its score goes up from 0 to +2). Copper gains those two electrons (gets reduced — its score goes down from +2 to 0). Zinc gave the ball away; copper caught it. The giver is oxidized; the catcher is reduced.
rationales.highYield: OIL RIG: Oxidation Is Loss of e-, Reduction Is Gain of e-. Oxidized species = reducing agent; reduced species = oxidizing agent.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: What is matter?

rationales.whyCorrect: Matter occupies space and has mass.
rationales.eli10: If it takes up room and can be weighed, it is matter.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which state has fixed shape and volume?

rationales.whyCorrect: Particles in a solid remain in fixed relative positions.
rationales.eli10: A solid keeps its own shape and size.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which is a chemical property?

rationales.whyCorrect: Flammability describes ability to undergo combustion.
rationales.eli10: It tells whether a substance can change by burning.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which is a physical change?

rationales.whyCorrect: Melting changes state without changing molecular identity.
rationales.eli10: Frozen water becomes liquid water but stays water.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which quantity measures amount of matter?

rationales.whyCorrect: Mass measures how much matter an object contains.
rationales.eli10: Mass tells how much stuff is there.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which instrument measures liquid volume accurately?

rationales.whyCorrect: Graduated cylinders have calibrated volume markings.
rationales.eli10: Its lines show how much liquid it holds.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Density equals:

rationales.whyCorrect: Density is mass per unit volume.
rationales.eli10: It asks how much stuff is packed into a space.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: What is the SI base unit of temperature?

rationales.whyCorrect: Kelvin is the SI base temperature unit.
rationales.eli10: Scientists use kelvins as the official temperature steps.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: How is 0.00045 written in scientific notation?

rationales.whyCorrect: Moving the decimal four places right gives exponent −4.
rationales.eli10: Scientific notation makes tiny numbers compact.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: How many milliliters are in 2.5 L?

rationales.whyCorrect: One liter equals 1,000 mL, so 2.5 × 1,000 = 2,500.
rationales.eli10: Each liter contains one thousand milliliters.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A sample has mass 20 g and volume 5 mL. Its density is:

rationales.whyCorrect: Density = 20 g ÷ 5 mL = 4 g/mL.
rationales.eli10: Twenty grams packed into five spaces gives four per space.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: How many significant figures are in 0.00450?

rationales.whyCorrect: Leading zeros are placeholders; the trailing zero after the decimal is significant.
rationales.eli10: Only 4, 5, and the measured ending zero count.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which is a physical property of ethanol?

rationales.whyCorrect: Boiling point can be measured without changing chemical identity.
rationales.eli10: You can measure when it boils without making a new substance.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which observation indicates a chemical change?

rationales.whyCorrect: Rust is a new substance produced by oxidation.
rationales.eli10: The metal turns into a different chemical material.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: How many meters are in 5.0 km?

rationales.whyCorrect: Multiply kilometers by 1,000 to obtain meters.
rationales.eli10: Five groups of one thousand meters make five kilometers.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: About what Celsius temperature equals 68°F?

rationales.eli10: A comfortable room is about twenty degrees Celsius.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Why are conversion factors useful in dimensional analysis?

rationales.whyCorrect: Equivalent-unit ratios equal one and cancel units algebraically.
rationales.eli10: Matching unit labels cross out like matching puzzle pieces.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: How should water volume be read in a glass cylinder?

options.text: At the meniscus bottom at eye level

rationales.whyCorrect: Eye-level reading of the lower meniscus reduces parallax error.
rationales.eli10: Look straight across at the bottom of the water's curve.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A balance displays 12.30 g. What place is directly measured last?

rationales.whyCorrect: The last displayed digit is in the 0.01-g place.
rationales.eli10: The final zero says the scale reads hundredths of a gram.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: What is the safer way to dilute concentrated acid?

rationales.whyCorrect: Adding acid to water disperses heat and reduces splashing risk.
rationales.eli10: Put the strong acid into lots of water a little at a time.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: What ordinary number equals 3.2 × 10³?

rationales.whyCorrect: A positive exponent of 3 moves the decimal three places right.
rationales.eli10: Three decimal jumps turn 3.2 into 3,200.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Convert 0.25 g to milligrams.

rationales.whyCorrect: Multiplying grams by 1,000 gives milligrams.
rationales.eli10: A quarter of one thousand milligrams is 250.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: An object floats in water because its average density is:

rationales.whyCorrect: Objects less dense than the fluid can float.
rationales.eli10: It packs less mass into its space than water does.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: When temperature rises, particles generally have:

rationales.whyCorrect: Temperature reflects average particle kinetic energy.
rationales.eli10: Hotter particles jiggle and travel faster.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Using significant figures, 12.1 × 3.42 equals:

rationales.whyCorrect: The raw product is 41.382 and both factors allow three significant figures.
rationales.eli10: Round the answer to the least detailed measurement: three useful digits.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Water has density 1.00 g/mL. What is the mass of 150 mL?

rationales.whyCorrect: Mass = density × volume = 150 g.
rationales.eli10: Each milliliter weighs about one gram.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Repeated measurements cluster closely but miss the accepted value. They are:

rationales.whyCorrect: Clustering shows precision; missing the true value shows inaccuracy.
rationales.eli10: The darts group together but away from the bull's-eye.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which evidence most strongly indicates a chemical reaction?

rationales.whyCorrect: Formation of an insoluble new substance signals chemical change.
rationales.eli10: A new solid appearing shows the ingredients rearranged.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: How can density of an irregular solid be measured?

options.text: Mass it and use water displacement for volume

rationales.whyCorrect: Mass divided by displaced-water volume gives density.
rationales.eli10: Weigh it, see how much water it pushes aside, then divide.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A scale always reads 0.8 g high. This is primarily:

rationales.whyCorrect: A consistent offset biases every measurement in the same direction.
rationales.eli10: The scale has the same crooked starting point each time.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which particle determines atomic number?

rationales.whyCorrect: Atomic number equals the number of protons.
rationales.eli10: Count the protons to learn the element's number.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Atoms of one element with different neutron counts are:

rationales.whyCorrect: Isotopes share proton number but differ in neutrons.
rationales.eli10: They are the same element wearing different neutron backpacks.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: An ion forms when an atom changes its number of:

rationales.whyCorrect: Electron gain or loss changes net charge.
rationales.eli10: Taking or adding negative pieces changes the atom's charge.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which electrons participate most in bonding?

rationales.whyCorrect: Outer-shell valence electrons interact between atoms.
rationales.eli10: The outside electrons are the atom's handshakes.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A horizontal row of the periodic table is a:

rationales.whyCorrect: Periods run horizontally and relate to occupied energy levels.
rationales.eli10: A period is one row across the table.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A vertical column of the periodic table is a:

rationales.whyCorrect: Elements in a group often share valence patterns.
rationales.eli10: A group is one family column.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which property is typical of metals?

rationales.whyCorrect: Mobile electrons make many metals good conductors.
rationales.eli10: Electricity travels easily through their shared electrons.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which element type commonly gains electrons?

rationales.whyCorrect: Nonmetals often gain electrons to complete valence shells.
rationales.eli10: They often collect outside electrons to fill their outer ring.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which class has properties between metals and nonmetals?

rationales.whyCorrect: Metalloids show intermediate or mixed properties.
rationales.eli10: They behave partly like each side of the table.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A positive ion is a:

rationales.whyCorrect: Loss of electrons leaves a net positive charge.
rationales.eli10: Losing negative pieces makes the atom positive.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Mass number equals:

rationales.whyCorrect: Nearly all atomic mass comes from protons and neutrons.
rationales.eli10: Add the heavy pieces in the nucleus.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Two carbon isotopes must have the same number of:

rationales.whyCorrect: All carbon atoms have six protons.
rationales.eli10: The proton name tag stays carbon even when neutrons differ.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: How many valence electrons does neutral chlorine usually have?

rationales.whyCorrect: Group 17 elements have seven valence electrons.
rationales.eli10: Chlorine needs one more to fill its outside ring of eight.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Why is sodium chemically reactive?

options.text: It has a full outer shell
It readily loses one valence electron

rationales.whyCorrect: Losing its lone outer electron gives sodium a stable configuration.
rationales.eli10: Sodium easily drops its one lonely outside electron.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Across a period from left to right, atomic radius generally:

rationales.whyCorrect: Increasing nuclear charge pulls electrons closer within the same shell.
rationales.eli10: A stronger center tug makes the atom smaller.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A neutral calcium atom has 20 electrons. How many does Ca²⁺ have?

rationales.whyCorrect: A 2+ charge means calcium lost two electrons.
rationales.eli10: Twenty negatives minus two leaves eighteen.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: An oxygen atom has atomic number 8. How many protons does it have?

rationales.whyCorrect: Atomic number directly states proton count.
rationales.eli10: Oxygen's number 8 means eight protons.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Sodium-23 has 11 protons. How many neutrons?

rationales.whyCorrect: Neutrons = mass number 23 − protons 11 = 12.
rationales.eli10: Take eleven proton blocks away from twenty-three heavy blocks.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Why do elements in one group often react similarly?

rationales.whyCorrect: Chemical behavior is governed largely by outer electrons.
rationales.eli10: Family members have similar outside-electron handshakes.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Why are noble gases relatively unreactive?

rationales.whyCorrect: Filled outer shells provide stable electron configurations.
rationales.eli10: Their outside seats are full, so they rarely trade electrons.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Compared with its neutral atom, a simple anion is often:

rationales.whyCorrect: Added electron repulsion expands the electron cloud.
rationales.eli10: Extra negative pieces crowd one another outward.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which ions combine in a neutral magnesium oxide formula?

rationales.whyCorrect: Equal opposite charges balance in a 1:1 ratio.
rationales.eli10: A plus two and minus two cancel perfectly.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: What primarily changes when moving down a periodic-table group?

options.text: The number of occupied electron shells

rationales.whyCorrect: Each lower period adds another main electron shell.
rationales.eli10: Moving down adds another electron layer.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which group contains the halogens?

rationales.whyCorrect: Fluorine, chlorine, and related halogens occupy group 17.
rationales.eli10: The salt-making family sits in column seventeen.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which group contains alkali metals?

rationales.whyCorrect: Alkali metals have one valence electron and occupy group 1.
rationales.eli10: The one-outside-electron metals fill the first column.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Electronegativity generally increases:

rationales.whyCorrect: Smaller atoms with higher effective nuclear charge attract bonds strongly.
rationales.eli10: Atoms near the top right tug shared electrons hardest.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Why is an element's listed atomic mass often decimal?

options.text: It is a weighted average of natural isotopes

rationales.whyCorrect: Natural isotope masses contribute according to abundance.
rationales.eli10: The table averages heavier and lighter versions by how common they are.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Why is potassium generally more reactive than lithium?

options.text: Its valence electron is farther from the nucleus

rationales.whyCorrect: Greater distance and shielding make potassium's outer electron easier to lose.
rationales.eli10: Potassium's outside electron is held by a longer, weaker leash.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: An element is shiny, malleable, and conductive. It is most likely a:

rationales.whyCorrect: Those physical properties characterize metallic bonding.
rationales.eli10: It acts like the bendable shiny wires metals make.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Why is periodic-table position useful?

options.text: It predicts valence and chemical behavior

rationales.whyCorrect: Periodic placement reflects electron configuration and recurring trends.
rationales.eli10: An element's address hints how it will make chemical friends.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: An ionic bond results mainly from:

rationales.whyCorrect: Oppositely charged ions attract after electrons transfer.
rationales.eli10: One atom gives an electron, and the new charges stick together.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A covalent bond forms when atoms:

rationales.whyCorrect: Shared valence electrons hold atoms together.
rationales.eli10: Atoms grip the same electron pair.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A polar covalent bond has:

rationales.whyCorrect: Different electronegativities pull shared electrons unequally.
rationales.eli10: One atom tugs the shared blanket harder.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which attraction occurs between water molecules?

rationales.whyCorrect: A partially positive hydrogen attracts a nearby oxygen.
rationales.eli10: The positive end of one tiny magnet likes another's negative end.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: What is electronegativity?

rationales.whyCorrect: Electronegativity measures an atom's pull within a bond.
rationales.eli10: It is how strongly an atom tugs the shared blanket.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: What is the formula for sodium chloride?

rationales.whyCorrect: Na+ and Cl− balance in a one-to-one ratio.
rationales.eli10: One plus and one minus pair evenly.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: What is the formula for calcium chloride?

rationales.whyCorrect: One Ca²⁺ requires two Cl− ions for neutrality.
rationales.eli10: A plus-two calcium needs two minus-one chlorides.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which substance is a molecular compound?

rationales.whyCorrect: Carbon and oxygen are nonmetals joined covalently in discrete molecules.
rationales.eli10: Carbon dioxide is a small group of shared-electron atoms.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A bond between two oxygen atoms is:

rationales.whyCorrect: Identical atoms share bonding electrons equally.
rationales.eli10: Equal twins tug the shared electrons equally.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Why is water polar overall?

options.text: Its bent shape leaves unequal charge distribution

rationales.whyCorrect: Bent geometry prevents bond dipoles from canceling.
rationales.eli10: Its V shape leaves one side a little negative.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Stronger intermolecular forces usually cause a liquid to have:

rationales.whyCorrect: More energy is needed to separate strongly attracted molecules.
rationales.eli10: Stickier molecules need more heat to pull apart.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Why can molten ionic compounds conduct electricity?

rationales.whyCorrect: Mobile charged ions carry current in the liquid state.
rationales.eli10: Melted charged pieces can travel and carry electricity.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Hydrogen bonds between DNA bases help:

rationales.whyCorrect: Many individually weak hydrogen bonds stabilize the double helix.
rationales.eli10: Tiny attractions act like zipper teeth between DNA rails.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: What is the correct name for CO2?

rationales.whyCorrect: The prefix di- indicates two oxygen atoms.
rationales.eli10: The name says one carbon with two oxygens.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: What is Na2O called?

rationales.whyCorrect: Ionic compounds name the metal then nonmetal with -ide.
rationales.eli10: Say the metal name, then turn oxygen into oxide.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: How many shared electron pairs form the O=O bond?

rationales.whyCorrect: A double covalent bond contains two shared pairs.
rationales.eli10: The double line means two electron handholds.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Why do many lipids avoid water?

rationales.whyCorrect: Nonpolar regions interact poorly with polar water.
rationales.eli10: Oily tails do not match water's tiny charges.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: What helps stabilize protein folding?

options.text: Hydrogen bonds and other side-chain attractions

rationales.whyCorrect: Multiple weak interactions help maintain three-dimensional protein shape.
rationales.eli10: Many tiny grips hold the folded protein together.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: What is methane's basic molecular shape?

rationales.whyCorrect: Four electron groups around carbon arrange tetrahedrally.
rationales.eli10: Four bonds point toward the corners of a tiny pyramid-like shape.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Why does water dissolve many salts?

rationales.whyCorrect: Polar water molecules form hydration shells around cations and anions.
rationales.eli10: Water's charged ends tug salt pieces apart and hug them.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Two similar molecules differ only in intermolecular strength. Which is more volatile?

options.text: The larger one regardless of bonding

rationales.whyCorrect: Weakly attracted molecules escape to vapor more easily.
rationales.eli10: Loosely held neighbors fly away sooner.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A bond's electrons spend more time near oxygen than hydrogen. The bond is:

rationales.whyCorrect: Unequal electron distribution creates partial charges without full transfer.
rationales.eli10: Oxygen pulls harder but still shares.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Soap can surround grease in water because soap molecules are:

rationales.whyCorrect: They have water-attracting heads and grease-attracting tails.
rationales.eli10: One end likes water while the other grabs oil.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Why are ionic solids often brittle?

options.text: Shifting layers aligns like charges that repel

rationales.whyCorrect: A displaced ionic lattice can bring equal charges together and fracture.
rationales.eli10: Slide the rows and matching charges push the crystal apart.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Why must both bond polarity and shape be considered for molecular polarity?

options.text: Bond dipoles may reinforce or cancel

rationales.whyCorrect: The spatial sum of bond dipoles determines overall polarity.
rationales.eli10: Tiny arrows can add together or point against each other.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: CO2 has polar bonds but is nonpolar because:

rationales.whyCorrect: Equal dipoles point in opposite directions in a linear molecule.
rationales.eli10: Two equal tugs pull opposite ways, giving no overall tug.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Why are weak bonds biologically valuable?

options.text: Many together stabilize structures yet allow change

rationales.whyCorrect: Reversible weak interactions support recognition, folding, and separation.
rationales.eli10: Many tiny fasteners hold well but can unzip when needed.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which change would most weaken an ionic interaction in water?

rationales.whyCorrect: Polar water reduces direct electrostatic attraction between ions.
rationales.eli10: Water crowds around charges and softens their pull.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: When NaCl dissolves, why do ions remain separated?

rationales.whyCorrect: Oriented water molecules surround and stabilize each charged ion.
rationales.eli10: Water coats each salt piece so they stay apart.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Breaking a stable chemical bond requires energy because:

rationales.whyCorrect: Energy must separate nuclei and electrons held at a low-energy distance.
rationales.eli10: You must spend effort to pull strongly joined pieces apart.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Why must chemical equations be balanced?

rationales.whyCorrect: Reactions rearrange atoms without creating or destroying them.
rationales.eli10: Every atom entering must appear somewhere after the change.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: In 2H2 + O2 → 2H2O, the coefficient of H2O is:

rationales.whyCorrect: The written coefficient 2 represents two formula units or moles.
rationales.eli10: The big number says two water groups form.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Substances present before a reaction are:

rationales.whyCorrect: Reactants are consumed or changed to form products.
rationales.eli10: They are the starting ingredients.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A + B → AB is what reaction type?

rationales.whyCorrect: Two simpler substances combine into one product.
rationales.eli10: Two pieces join to make one larger piece.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A compound separates into simpler substances during heating. How is the reaction classified?

rationales.whyCorrect: One compound splits into simpler products.
rationales.eli10: One built object comes apart.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A + BC → AC + B is a:

rationales.whyCorrect: One element displaces another within a compound.
rationales.eli10: One outsider takes another's place.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: AB + CD → AD + CB is a:

rationales.whyCorrect: Two compounds exchange ionic partners.
rationales.eli10: Two couples swap partners.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Complete hydrocarbon combustion produces mainly:

rationales.whyCorrect: Carbon oxidizes to CO2 and hydrogen to H2O.
rationales.eli10: Burning fuel fully makes carbon dioxide and water.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: One mole contains approximately:

rationales.whyCorrect: Avogadro's number defines the particle count in a mole.
rationales.eli10: A mole is a giant counting bundle.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: What is the approximate molar mass of H2O?

rationales.whyCorrect: Two hydrogens contribute about 2 and oxygen about 16 g/mol.
rationales.eli10: Add two ones and one sixteen.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: How many moles are in 36 g of water?

rationales.whyCorrect: Moles = 36 g ÷ 18 g/mol = 2.
rationales.eli10: Thirty-six grams contains two eighteen-gram bundles.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: What mass is 0.50 mol NaCl if its molar mass is 58.5 g/mol?

rationales.eli10: Half a mole weighs half of 58.5 grams.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: What is the limiting reactant?

rationales.whyCorrect: It limits product because it runs out first.
rationales.eli10: The ingredient that empties first limits how many cookies you bake.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Balanced-equation coefficients provide:

rationales.whyCorrect: Coefficients relate amounts of reactants and products in moles.
rationales.eli10: They are the recipe's batch proportions.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which equation is balanced?

rationales.whyCorrect: Both sides contain two N atoms and six H atoms.
rationales.eli10: The atom counts match before and after.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: How many moles O2 react with 1 mol CH4 in CH4 + 2O2 → CO2 + 2H2O?

rationales.whyCorrect: The coefficient ratio is 2 mol O2 per 1 mol CH4.
rationales.eli10: The recipe asks for two oxygen bundles per methane bundle.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Mixing two clear ionic solutions forms a solid. The solid is a:

rationales.whyCorrect: An insoluble reaction product that appears from solution is a precipitate.
rationales.eli10: Dissolved pieces join and fall out as a solid.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A sealed reaction's total mass stays constant because:

rationales.whyCorrect: Conservation of mass follows conservation of atoms in ordinary reactions.
rationales.eli10: The same building blocks are simply rebuilt.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: 2Na + Cl2 → 2NaCl is classified as:

rationales.whyCorrect: Two elements combine to form one compound type.
rationales.eli10: Two starting materials join into salt.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: If 3 mol H2 require 1 mol N2, how much N2 is needed for 6 mol H2?

rationales.whyCorrect: Doubling hydrogen from 3 to 6 mol doubles nitrogen from 1 to 2 mol.
rationales.eli10: Twice the recipe needs twice each ingredient.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A reaction yields less product than predicted. Percent yield is:

rationales.whyCorrect: Percent yield compares recovered product with the stoichiometric maximum.
rationales.eli10: It tells what fraction of the hoped-for product you got.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: In 2H2O2 → 2H2O + O2, 2 mol H2O2 can form:

rationales.whyCorrect: The coefficient ratio is 2 mol peroxide to 1 mol oxygen.
rationales.eli10: Two peroxide bundles make one oxygen-gas bundle.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Why should coefficients, not subscripts, be changed when balancing?

rationales.whyCorrect: Coefficients change amount; subscripts change chemical formulas.
rationales.eli10: Add more whole molecules without rebuilding each molecule.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which observation best identifies a gas-producing reaction?

rationales.whyCorrect: New bubbles at constant temperature can indicate gaseous product.
rationales.eli10: Fizzing may show the reaction made a gas.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: For 2A + B → C, 5 mol A and 4 mol B are available. Which limits product?

rationales.whyCorrect: Five moles A can react with only 2.5 mol B, so A runs out first.
rationales.eli10: The recipe needs two A pieces each time, so A empties sooner.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: For the same reaction, how many moles C can 5 mol A produce?

rationales.whyCorrect: The 2:1 ratio gives 5 ÷ 2 = 2.5 mol C.
rationales.eli10: Every two A bundles make one C bundle.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A sample contains 3.01 × 10²³ molecules. This is about:

rationales.whyCorrect: This count is half of Avogadro's number.
rationales.eli10: Half the giant particle bundle is half a mole.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Why can excess reactant remain after a reaction stops?

options.text: The limiting reactant has been exhausted

rationales.whyCorrect: No more product forms when one required reactant is gone.
rationales.eli10: Extra flour remains when the eggs run out.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A 10.0-g reactant forms 8.0 g product and 2.0 g gas. What does this show?

rationales.whyCorrect: Product masses total the original 10.0 g.
rationales.eli10: Eight plus two accounts for all ten grams.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: If a balanced equation is doubled, what changes?

rationales.whyCorrect: Scaling a reaction changes batch size while preserving proportions.
rationales.eli10: Doubling a recipe keeps the same ingredient ratios.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: What is the dissolved substance in a solution?

rationales.whyCorrect: The solute disperses within the solvent.
rationales.eli10: The solute is the ingredient being mixed in.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: What is the dissolving medium called?

rationales.whyCorrect: The solvent is the component that dissolves the solute.
rationales.eli10: The solvent is the larger liquid home for the dissolved ingredient.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: An aqueous solution uses which solvent?

rationales.whyCorrect: Aqueous means dissolved in water.
rationales.eli10: Aqua is a clue that water is the mixing liquid.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: What does solubility describe?

options.text: Maximum solute that can dissolve under stated conditions

rationales.whyCorrect: Solubility is an equilibrium amount dependent on conditions.
rationales.eli10: It is how much ingredient the liquid can hold.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Molarity is:

rationales.whyCorrect: M = moles of solute divided by total solution liters.
rationales.eli10: Count chemical bundles in each liter.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which solution conducts because it contains mobile ions?

rationales.whyCorrect: Electrolytes dissociate or ionize into charged particles.
rationales.eli10: Moving charged pieces carry electricity through the liquid.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which substance is usually a nonelectrolyte in water?

rationales.whyCorrect: Glucose dissolves as neutral molecules rather than ions.
rationales.eli10: Sugar mixes in but does not split into charged pieces.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: What is dilution?

rationales.whyCorrect: Dilution spreads the same solute amount through more solution.
rationales.eli10: Add water so each cup contains less ingredient.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which expression calculates molarity?

rationales.whyCorrect: Molarity directly relates amount in moles to volume in liters.
rationales.eli10: Divide chemical bundles by liters.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: What is the molarity of 0.50 mol solute in 2.0 L?

rationales.eli10: Half a bundle spread across two liters gives a quarter per liter.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: 100 mL of 1.0 M solution is diluted to 500 mL. Final concentration?

rationales.eli10: Five times the volume makes the mixture five times weaker.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A 5% w/v solution contains:

rationales.whyCorrect: Percent weight/volume means grams in each 100 mL.
rationales.eli10: Five percent means five grams in one hundred milliliters.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A saturated solution has:

options.text: The maximum dissolved solute at those conditions

rationales.whyCorrect: At saturation, extra solute does not dissolve at equilibrium.
rationales.eli10: The liquid's dissolved-ingredient seats are full.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: For many solids, warming the solvent generally:

rationales.whyCorrect: Many solid solutes dissolve to a greater extent at higher temperature.
rationales.eli10: Warm liquid can often hold more solid ingredient.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Water evaporates from a salt solution. Salt concentration usually:

rationales.whyCorrect: Solvent decreases while nonvolatile solute remains.
rationales.eli10: The same salt is squeezed into less water.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: An IV fluid has fewer effective particles than cell fluid. It is:

rationales.whyCorrect: A hypotonic solution has lower effective osmolarity than cells.
rationales.eli10: The outside is less crowded with trapped particles.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: What does osmolarity count?

rationales.whyCorrect: Osmolarity reflects all osmotically active particles per liter.
rationales.eli10: It counts every separate dissolved piece pulling on water.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: At equal molarity, why can NaCl have greater osmolarity than glucose?

rationales.whyCorrect: One NaCl unit ideally produces Na+ and Cl− particles.
rationales.eli10: Salt splits into two water-pulling pieces; sugar stays one.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A 0.9% w/v NaCl label means:

rationales.whyCorrect: Weight/volume percent states grams per 100 mL solution.
rationales.eli10: Each hundred milliliters contains nine-tenths of a gram.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which action lowers a solution's molarity without removing solute?

rationales.whyCorrect: Increasing volume around the same solute lowers moles per liter.
rationales.eli10: Spread the same syrup through more water.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: How much 2.0 M stock is needed to make 100 mL of 0.50 M solution?

rationales.eli10: The stock is four times stronger, so use one-fourth of the final volume.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A liquid contains 250 mg per 5 mL. How much is in 10 mL?

rationales.whyCorrect: Ten milliliters is twice five, so the amount doubles.
rationales.eli10: Two spoonful-sized portions contain two times the drug.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Stirring a solid in water usually changes:

rationales.whyCorrect: Stirring brings fresh solvent to the surface but often not the saturation limit.
rationales.eli10: Stirring fills the seats faster without adding seats.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: When dissolved ions form an insoluble compound, it appears as a:

rationales.whyCorrect: The insoluble product separates from solution as a solid.
rationales.eli10: The dissolved pieces join and fall out.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: What is the molarity of 5.85 g NaCl (58.5 g/mol) in 0.500 L?

rationales.eli10: One-tenth bundle in half a liter equals two-tenths per liter.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Ideally, one mole of CaCl2 yields how many osmoles of particles?

rationales.whyCorrect: CaCl2 dissociates into one Ca²⁺ and two Cl− ions.
rationales.eli10: One unit breaks into three separate pieces.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Cells placed in a strongly hypertonic solution will:

rationales.whyCorrect: Water moves toward the more concentrated external solution.
rationales.eli10: Water leaves the cells for the more crowded outside.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Why does an isotonic fluid preserve cell volume?

rationales.whyCorrect: Balanced tonicity produces no sustained net water shift.
rationales.eli10: Equal water pulls keep the cell's size steady.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Two successive 1:10 dilutions create what total dilution?

rationales.whyCorrect: Dilution factors multiply: 10×10=100.
rationales.eli10: Making it ten times weaker twice makes it one hundred times weaker.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Why must medication concentrations include units?

options.text: Units distinguish amounts such as mg/mL from mg/L
All concentrations use the same scale

rationales.whyCorrect: A bare number cannot specify the amount-to-volume relationship safely.
rationales.eli10: The label needs to say what each number counts.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A Brønsted acid donates:

rationales.whyCorrect: A Brønsted-Lowry acid is a proton donor.
rationales.eli10: An acid can hand off an H+ piece.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A Brønsted base accepts:

rationales.whyCorrect: A Brønsted-Lowry base accepts protons.
rationales.eli10: A base has a spot that can catch H+.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: At 25°C, neutral water has pH:

rationales.whyCorrect: Equal H+ and OH− concentrations give pH 7.
rationales.eli10: Seven is the middle balance point.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: As pH decreases, hydrogen-ion concentration:

rationales.whyCorrect: pH is the negative logarithm of H+ concentration.
rationales.eli10: A smaller pH number means more acid particles.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A strong acid in water:

rationales.whyCorrect: Strong acids transfer nearly all available protons to water.
rationales.eli10: Almost every acid molecule lets go of its H+.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A weak acid:

rationales.whyCorrect: Many weak-acid molecules remain un-ionized in water.
rationales.eli10: Only some molecules hand off their H+ at a time.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Acid-base neutralization commonly forms:

rationales.whyCorrect: H+ and OH− form water while remaining ions form salt.
rationales.eli10: Opposite acid and base pieces meet and calm each other.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: What is a buffer's main function?

rationales.whyCorrect: A buffer binds added acid or base within a working range.
rationales.eli10: It softens pushes that would change acidity.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which buffer is important in blood?

rationales.whyCorrect: The carbonic acid-bicarbonate system helps regulate blood pH.
rationales.eli10: Bicarbonate is part of the blood's acidity shock absorber.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A pH 3 solution has how much more H+ than pH 5?

rationales.whyCorrect: A two-unit difference equals 10², or 100-fold.
rationales.eli10: Each pH step multiplies acidity by ten.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Adding equal reactive amounts of strong acid and strong base mainly causes:

rationales.whyCorrect: Stoichiometric H+ and OH− combine to form water.
rationales.eli10: The acid and base pieces cancel each other.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A blood pH below its normal range is called:

rationales.whyCorrect: Acidosis describes excessive acidity relative to the physiologic range.
rationales.eli10: The blood has moved too far toward the acid side.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Retention of carbon dioxide tends to increase:

rationales.whyCorrect: CO2 hydration forms carbonic acid, which can release H+.
rationales.eli10: Trapped waste gas can make the fluid more acidic.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A primary decrease in bicarbonate is associated conceptually with:

rationales.whyCorrect: Bicarbonate loss reduces a major base component.
rationales.eli10: Losing part of the base buffer tips toward acid.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: How does a buffer respond to added H+?

options.text: Its base component binds some H+

rationales.whyCorrect: The conjugate base converts added H+ into weak acid.
rationales.eli10: The buffer catches extra acid pieces.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A pH 12 solution has how much more OH− than pH 10?

rationales.whyCorrect: Each pH increase corresponds to a tenfold OH− increase; two steps give 100.
rationales.eli10: Two ruler steps mean one hundred times more base particles.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: At equal concentration, which generally has the lower pH?

rationales.whyCorrect: More complete ionization produces a higher H+ concentration.
rationales.eli10: The strong acid releases more H+ pieces.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Why can a weak acid help form a buffer?

options.text: It coexists with its conjugate base

rationales.whyCorrect: The reversible pair can consume added base or acid.
rationales.eli10: One partner can catch acid, and the other can catch base.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Faster ventilation that lowers CO2 tends to:

rationales.whyCorrect: Less CO2 shifts the carbonic-acid system toward lower H+.
rationales.eli10: Blowing off acid-making gas moves pH upward.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which organ provides slower regulation by adjusting H+ and bicarbonate excretion?

rationales.whyCorrect: Kidneys regulate acid-base balance through tubular transport.
rationales.eli10: Kidneys sort acid and buffer pieces into urine or blood.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Two acids have equal concentration but different pH. What likely differs?

rationales.whyCorrect: Stronger ionization produces more H+ at the same formal concentration.
rationales.eli10: One acid lets go of more H+ pieces.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: An antacid raises stomach pH by:

rationales.whyCorrect: Basic antacid components consume hydrogen ions.
rationales.eli10: It uses base pieces to calm some stomach acid.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A buffer is most effective when pH is near its:

rationales.whyCorrect: Near pKa, useful amounts of acid and conjugate base coexist.
rationales.eli10: The buffer works best when both helper partners are available.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Why can extreme pH harm proteins?

options.text: It disrupts ionic and hydrogen interactions

rationales.whyCorrect: Altered side-chain charges can unfold or inactivate proteins.
rationales.eli10: Too much acid or base loosens the tiny grips holding protein shape.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: If [H+] = 1 × 10⁻⁴ M, pH equals:

rationales.eli10: The exponent's four becomes the pH number.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: If pH changes from 7.4 to 7.1, the fluid became:

rationales.whyCorrect: A lower pH reflects a higher hydrogen-ion concentration.
rationales.eli10: The pH ruler moved toward the acid end.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A person hypoventilates and CO2 rises. Which initial chemical shift occurs?

rationales.whyCorrect: The equilibrium CO2 + H2O ⇌ H2CO3 shifts toward carbonic acid.
rationales.eli10: More gas pushes the acid-making reaction forward.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Why can buffers not prevent unlimited pH change?

rationales.whyCorrect: Once buffer components are depleted, additional acid or base shifts pH sharply.
rationales.eli10: A sponge stops helping after it is full.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A solution resists added acid but not added base. What is likely depleted?

rationales.whyCorrect: The weak acid is needed to neutralize added base.
rationales.eli10: The base-catching half of the team has run out.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which statement integrates respiratory and metabolic acid-base control?

options.text: Lungs regulate CO2; kidneys regulate H+ and bicarbonate

subjectWideQuestions.stem: An atom contains 15 protons, 16 neutrons, and 15 electrons. Which statement correctly identifies this atom's mass number and what that number represents?

options.text: 15, the number of protons in the nucleus
31, the total number of protons and neutrons in the nucleus
16, the number of neutrons in the nucleus
30, the total number of protons and electrons in the atom

rationales.whyCorrect: Mass number (A) is the nucleon count, protons plus neutrons, so 15 + 16 = 31. The atomic number (Z = 15) counts protons alone and fixes the element's identity (phosphorus), while electrons are roughly 1/1836 the mass of a nucleon and are excluded from the mass number. Separating A from Z is the prerequisite for reading isotope notation and for calculating neutrons as A minus Z.
rationales.eli10: Two different counts get confused all the time. The atomic number counts only protons, and it decides which element you have. The mass number counts everything heavy in the nucleus, protons plus neutrons together, because those are the particles that actually weigh something. Electrons are so light they do not change the total in any meaningful way. So here: 15 protons plus 16 neutrons gives a mass number of 31, while the atomic number stays 15.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Carbon-12 and carbon-14 each contain 6 protons, but carbon-14 contains 8 neutrons. Which term best describes the relationship between these two atoms, and why?

options.text: Isotopes, atoms of one element that differ in neutron number
Allotropes, different structural forms built from the same element
Ions, atoms of one element that differ in electron number
Isomers, substances with the same formula but different atomic arrangements

rationales.whyCorrect: Both atoms have Z = 6, so both are carbon; carbon-14 simply carries two extra neutrons (14 - 6 = 8 versus 12 - 6 = 6). Atoms of one element that differ only in neutron count are isotopes, and because their electron configurations are identical their chemical behavior is essentially the same. Ions differ in electron count and therefore carry charge, allotropes are different bonding arrangements of an element such as graphite versus diamond, and isomers are compounds with identical formulas but different structures.
rationales.eli10: The proton count is what makes an atom carbon, and it never changes without changing the element itself. Neutrons are different: they add mass to the nucleus but no charge, so you can add or subtract a couple and still have carbon. Carbon-14 carries 8 neutrons instead of the usual 6, which makes it heavier but chemically the same substance. Versions of one element that differ only in neutron count are called isotopes.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Fluorine, chlorine, and bromine all appear in Group 17 of the periodic table. Which statement best explains why these three elements show similar chemical behavior?

options.text: They occupy the same period, so their valence electrons fill the same principal energy level
They have nearly equal atomic masses, so their nuclei exert similar attraction
They have equal numbers of core electrons, so the same nuclear pull reaches each outer shell
They each hold 7 valence electrons, so they gain or share electrons in similar ways

rationales.whyCorrect: For main-group elements the group number gives the valence electron count; Group 17 members have 17 - 10 = 7 electrons in the outermost shell. Chemical behavior is governed almost entirely by valence electrons, so all three need one additional electron to reach an octet and react in parallel ways. They sit in different periods (n = 2, 3, and 4), have very different atomic masses, and have different core electron counts (2, 10, and 28), so none of those features can explain the shared chemistry.
rationales.eli10: Elements in the same column of the periodic table are grouped there for a reason: they have the same number of electrons in their outermost shell. Fluorine, chlorine, and bromine each have 7 outer electrons and each need just one more to reach the stable set of 8. That single shared gap is what makes them react in similar ways, even though the atoms differ greatly in size and mass. Outer electrons drive chemistry; the deeper electrons and the neutrons do not.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A proton has a mass of about 1.00728 amu and an electron about 0.00054858 amu. Which statement best explains why an atom's mass is treated as residing almost entirely in its nucleus?

options.text: Electrons are massless particles, so only nucleons can contribute to the mass of an atom
Electrons are excluded from mass totals because they carry negative rather than positive charge
A proton is roughly 1,836 times as massive as an electron, so protons and neutrons supply nearly all of the mass
The nucleus occupies most of the atom's volume, so it necessarily holds most of the atom's mass

rationales.whyCorrect: Dividing the two masses gives 1.00728 / 0.00054858, or about 1,836, and a neutron is slightly heavier still than a proton. In a carbon-12 atom the six electrons together contribute roughly 0.03 percent of the total mass, which is why mass number counts only nucleons. Charge is unrelated to mass; electrons have small but real mass; and the nucleus is about 100,000 times smaller in radius than the atom, so it holds nearly all the mass in a tiny fraction of the volume.
rationales.eli10: It takes about 1,836 electrons stacked together to match the mass of one proton. Neutrons weigh about the same as protons, so every particle in the nucleus is a heavyweight and every electron outside it is a featherweight. Even in a large atom with dozens of electrons, all of them together still add up to a rounding error compared with the nucleus. That is why chemists count only protons and neutrons when they talk about an atom's mass, and why the tiny nucleus carries nearly all of the weight despite taking up almost none of the space.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which comparison of maximum electron capacity between the second (n = 2) and third (n = 3) principal energy levels is accurate?

options.text: The n = 3 level holds 18 electrons, 10 more than n = 2, since capacity follows the 2n^2 relationship
The n = 3 level holds 16 electrons, 8 more than n = 2, since each level doubles the one before it
The n = 3 level holds 8 electrons, the same as n = 2, since an octet fills every principal level
The n = 3 level holds 12 electrons, 4 more than n = 2, since each level adds a single orbital

rationales.whyCorrect: Maximum occupancy of a principal energy level is 2n^2, giving 2(2^2) = 8 for n = 2 and 2(3^2) = 18 for n = 3, a difference of 10 electrons. Those 10 additional slots are the five d orbitals that first become available at n = 3, which is why a transition series contains 10 elements. Capacity is not the same as row length: because 4s fills before 3d, the 3d orbitals are not occupied until the fourth period (scandium through zinc), so the third period contains only 8 elements even though n = 3 can hold 18. The octet rule describes the stable valence arrangement of main-group elements, not the absolute capacity of a shell.
rationales.eli10: Each principal energy level has a fixed number of electron spots, and the formula is 2 times the level number squared. Level 2 gives 2 x 4 = 8 spots. Level 3 gives 2 x 9 = 18 spots. The 10 extra spots at level 3 come from a new set of five d orbitals that did not exist at level 2, and each orbital holds 2 electrons. Careful, though: having the spots is not the same as filling them right away. Electrons fill the 4s orbital before the 3d ones, so those 10 d spots do not get used until the fourth row of the periodic table, where you see the block of 10 transition metals from scandium to zinc. That is why the third row has only 8 elements even though level 3 can hold 18.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Atomic radius decreases steadily across Period 3, from sodium (Z = 11) to chlorine (Z = 17). Which explanation best accounts for this trend?

options.text: Each added electron enters a new principal energy level, so shielding grows faster than nuclear charge
Nuclear charge rises by 6 protons while electrons fill the same energy level, pulling the valence shell inward
Neutron count rises from 12 to 18, and the heavier nucleus compresses the surrounding electron cloud inward
Electron-electron repulsion falls as the 3p subshell fills, letting the outer shell relax closer to the nucleus

rationales.whyCorrect: Across Period 3 the added electrons all enter the n = 3 shell and shield one another poorly, while nuclear charge climbs from 11 to 17, an increase of 6 protons. Effective nuclear charge therefore rises left to right, tightening the pull on the valence electrons and shrinking the radius. Shielding grows only slightly and never outpaces the added protons, no new shell opens until Period 4, neutrons add mass but no charge and do not attract electrons, and filling the 3p subshell increases rather than decreases mutual repulsion.
rationales.eli10: Going across a row, you add one proton and one electron at a time, but the new electrons all land in the same outer shell rather than starting a new one farther out. Electrons in the same shell are poor at blocking each other from the nucleus, so the growing positive charge in the center is felt more and more strongly by the outer electrons. Stronger pull on electrons that are not moving farther out means the whole atom is drawn in tighter. That is why atoms get smaller as you move to the right, even though they are gaining particles.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which comparison between a neutral calcium atom (Z = 20) and a calcium ion carrying a 2+ charge is accurate?

options.text: The ion has 18 protons and 20 electrons, and that imbalance produces its 2+ charge
The ion has 22 electrons, gained in order to complete its outermost shell
Both particles have 20 electrons, but the ion contains 2 fewer neutrons
Both particles have 20 protons, but the ion has 18 electrons, leaving a net charge of 2+

rationales.whyCorrect: Ion formation changes only the electron count; the proton count stays at 20 or the particle would no longer be calcium. Losing the two 4s valence electrons leaves 20 positive charges against 18 negative ones, a net of 20 - 18 = 2+, and gives an argon-like arrangement. Note also that extra electrons would create a negative charge, not a positive one, and that neutron count is unaffected by ionization; this is why electrolytes such as calcium, sodium, and potassium circulate as charged particles while remaining the same elements.
rationales.eli10: Protons sit in the nucleus and are not removed in ordinary chemistry; changing them would change the element. Electrons sit on the outside and can be lost or gained fairly easily. Calcium gives up its two outermost electrons, so it still has 20 protons but now only 18 electrons, and the two unmatched positive charges are what the 2+ symbol means. The neutrons are untouched, so the ion has the same mass number as the atom it came from.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A hypothetical teaching sample is labeled as the potassium-39 ion with a 1+ charge (atomic number 19, mass number 39). How many neutrons and electrons does one of these ions contain?

rationales.whyCorrect: Neutron count equals mass number minus atomic number: 39 - 19 = 20. The 1+ charge means one electron has been lost from the neutral count of 19, leaving 18 electrons, an argon-like arrangement. Reading isotope and ion notation as two independent pieces of information, one nuclear and one electronic, is what allows correct interpretation of electrolyte chemistry, where potassium circulates as a singly charged cation.
rationales.eli10: There are two separate calculations hidden in this label, and each uses a different number. For neutrons, subtract the atomic number from the mass number: 39 minus 19 gives 20 neutrons. For electrons, start from the proton count, 19, and adjust for charge: a 1+ means one electron was lost, so 18 remain. The mass number tells you nothing about electrons, and the charge tells you nothing about neutrons, so never let one substitute for the other.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: An unidentified neutral element has electrons distributed as 2, 8, 2 across its first three shells. Which prediction about its periodic placement and bonding behavior is best supported?

options.text: Period 2, Group 2; it loses 2 electrons to form a 2+ cation
Period 3, Group 2; it loses 2 electrons to form a 2+ cation
Period 3, Group 2; it gains 6 electrons to complete an octet, forming a 6- anion
Period 3, Group 12; it shares both valence electrons and forms no ions

rationales.whyCorrect: Summing the shells gives 2 + 8 + 2 = 12 electrons in a neutral atom, so Z = 12 and the element is magnesium. The highest occupied shell is n = 3, which sets the period at 3, and the 2 valence electrons place it in Group 2, not Group 12 (the group number is not the atomic number). Alkaline earth metals have low ionization energies, so shedding 2 electrons to reach a neon-like configuration is far more favorable than gaining 6, producing the 2+ cation found in body fluids.
rationales.eli10: Start by adding up the electrons: 2 + 8 + 2 = 12, so a neutral atom of this element also has 12 protons, making it magnesium. The period number is simply the highest shell in use, which is shell 3. The group number for a main-group element comes from the valence electrons, and there are 2 on that outer shell, so Group 2. Then ask which is easier: losing 2 electrons or finding 6 more. Losing 2 wins, so this atom forms a 2+ ion.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A data table for a hypothetical element lists two isotopes: mass 63 amu at 69.2 percent abundance and mass 65 amu at 30.8 percent abundance. Which value is closest to the average atomic mass, and what does the result indicate?

options.text: 63 amu; the tabulated mass is set by the most abundant isotope alone
65 amu; the heavier isotope contributes more mass and therefore dominates
64 amu; the average is the midpoint between the two isotope masses
63.6 amu; the average sits nearer 63 because that isotope is more abundant

rationales.whyCorrect: Converting percentages to decimals and weighting each mass gives (0.692)(63) + (0.308)(65) = 63.62 amu, or about 63.6. The value must fall between the two isotope masses, and it shifts toward the more abundant lighter isotope rather than landing on the midpoint of 64 or on either isotope mass exactly. Checking that a weighted average lies between the extremes and leans toward the dominant component is a quick way to catch arithmetic errors.
rationales.eli10: A weighted average asks not just what the values are but how many of each you have. Here nearly 70 percent of the atoms weigh 63 and only about 30 percent weigh 65, so the light group pulls the average down toward its own value. Multiply each mass by its share as a decimal and add: 0.692 x 63 = 43.6 and 0.308 x 65 = 20, for a total near 63.6. Two quick checks: the answer must land between 63 and 65, and it must sit closer to whichever isotope is more common.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Element M has 11 protons (Period 3, Group 1) and element Q has 19 protons (Period 4, Group 1). What happens to the first ionization energy going from M to Q, and why?

options.text: Higher for Q, because 8 additional protons raise the nuclear charge felt by the valence electron
Identical for both, because each atom has only a single valence electron to remove
Lower for Q, because its valence electron occupies the fourth shell behind 8 more core electrons
Lower for Q, because its greater atomic mass weakens the nucleus's hold on the outer electron

rationales.whyCorrect: Element Q has 18 core electrons versus 10 for element M, a difference of 8 shielding electrons, and its lone valence electron sits in the n = 4 shell rather than n = 3. Greater distance plus increased shielding lowers the effective nuclear charge acting on that electron, so less energy is needed to remove it, even though total nuclear charge is larger. Mass itself exerts no electrostatic attraction, and having one valence electron does not by itself fix ionization energy, which is why first ionization energy falls down a group and the heavier alkali metals are the more reactive ones.
rationales.eli10: Both atoms have exactly one loose outer electron, so the difference has to come from how tightly that electron is held. In Q, the electron sits one shell farther out, and electrostatic attraction weakens sharply with distance. On top of that, 8 extra inner electrons stand between it and the nucleus, cancelling much of the positive pull it would otherwise feel. The net pull, called effective nuclear charge, is weaker for Q, so its electron leaves more easily and its ionization energy is lower.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Two hypothetical laboratory nuclide samples each contain neutral atoms with 53 protons; sample 1 has mass number 127 and sample 2 has mass number 131. Which statement best integrates the nuclear and chemical properties of these two samples?

options.text: They are isotopes: matching proton and electron counts give nearly identical chemistry, while the 4-neutron difference alters nuclear stability
They are different elements, because mass number rather than proton count establishes elemental identity and therefore reactivity
They are ions of one element, because adding neutrons to a nucleus changes the net charge carried by each sample
They are isotopes, but the added neutrons require added valence electrons, so the two samples form different chemical bonds

rationales.whyCorrect: Both samples have Z = 53, so both are the same element, and neutral atoms of each carry 53 electrons with identical valence configurations, making their chemical reactions essentially indistinguishable. Their neutron counts differ by 131 - 127 = 4, and the neutron-to-proton ratio governs nuclear stability, so one nuclide can be stable while the other decays. Neutrons are uncharged and do not affect electron count, and elemental identity is set by protons, not by mass number; this separation of chemical identity from nuclear behavior is why a radioactive nuclide follows the same biological pathway as its stable counterpart.
rationales.eli10: An atom really has two independent identities. The outside identity, set by protons and the matching electrons, decides how it bonds and where the body sends it, and both samples are identical there with 53 of each. The inside identity is set by the mix of protons and neutrons in the nucleus, and the two samples differ by 4 neutrons. Certain neutron-to-proton ratios hold together and others do not, so one nuclide can sit there indefinitely while the other breaks down and emits radiation. Same chemistry, different nuclear stability.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: An aluminum atom has 13 protons and 13 electrons. If it loses 3 electrons during a chemical reaction, which term and charge correctly describe the resulting particle?

options.text: An anion carrying a 3- charge, because removing electrons leaves the particle negative
An isotope carrying a 3+ charge, because the number of nuclear particles has changed
A cation carrying a 3+ charge, because protons now outnumber electrons by three
A cation carrying a 13+ charge, because all 13 protons are now unopposed

rationales.whyCorrect: Net ionic charge equals protons minus electrons: 13 - 10 = +3. A positively charged ion is a cation, and cations form by losing electrons. The 10 remaining electrons still cancel 10 of the 13 protons, so the charge is 3+, not 13+. Isotopes differ in neutron count, and the proton count (element identity) does not change in a chemical reaction, so the species is Al3+.
rationales.eli10: Charge is a subtraction problem, not a count of what is left. Protons are fixed at 13 and each one contributes +1; each electron contributes -1. Start at 13 plus and 13 minus, which cancel to zero. Remove 3 electrons and you have 13 plus against 10 minus, so 10 pairs cancel and 3 pluses survive: a 3+ charge. Any positively charged ion is a cation (the 't' in cation is a handy stand-in for a plus sign), and losing electrons is the only way an atom becomes one.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Magnesium chloride (MgCl2) is classified as a strong electrolyte. Which statement best explains that classification and the moles of ions released per mole dissolved?

options.text: It dissociates only slightly, so a small equilibrium fraction of ions carries nearly all of the current
It dissociates essentially completely, releasing 3 mol of mobile ions per mole, so the solution conducts well
It dissolves as intact neutral units that reorient in the electric field and conduct by shifting polar bonds
It dissociates completely but releases 2 mol of ions per mole, since each unit gives one cation and one anion

rationales.whyCorrect: A strong electrolyte is defined by essentially complete dissociation into free, mobile ions, which are the charge carriers that make a solution conduct. Each MgCl2 formula unit supplies one Mg2+ and two Cl-, so 1 + 2 = 3 mol of ions per mole of solute. Partial dissociation describes a weak electrolyte (for example acetic acid), and dissolving without dissociating describes a nonelectrolyte such as glucose.
rationales.eli10: Two ideas are bundled here. First, conduction needs charged particles that are free to move; a strong electrolyte supplies them because it comes apart essentially completely in water. Second, count the ions from the formula, not from the number of ion types: MgCl2 has one Mg and two Cl written into it, so one formula unit yields three separate particles. Weak electrolytes come apart only a little, and nonelectrolytes not at all, which is why their solutions conduct poorly or not at all.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A physiology text lists the normal serum reference interval for the major extracellular cation as 135-145 mEq/L. Which ion is being described, and what is the midpoint of that interval?

options.text: Potassium (K+), midpoint 140 mEq/L, because K+ is the dominant cation of extracellular fluid
Calcium (Ca2+), midpoint 140 mEq/L, because Ca2+ is the chief cation dissolved in plasma
Sodium (Na+), midpoint 140 mEq/L, because Na+ is the dominant cation of extracellular fluid
Sodium (Na+), midpoint 280 mEq/L, because the two interval endpoints are added together

rationales.whyCorrect: Sodium is the principal extracellular cation, and the midpoint of its reference interval is the mean of the endpoints: (135 + 145)/2 = 140 mEq/L. Adding the endpoints without dividing gives 280, a unit-nonsensical value. Potassium is the principal intracellular cation and circulates at only about 3.5-5 mEq/L, and although calcium is the most abundant cation in the body by mass, over 99% of it is bound in bone rather than dissolved in plasma (total serum calcium is roughly 4.5-5.5 mEq/L).
rationales.eli10: Two separate skills are being checked. The identity part rests on compartments: sodium is concentrated in the fluid outside cells, potassium inside cells, which is why a blood sample is dominated by sodium. The arithmetic part is a midpoint, which is an average, not a sum: add 135 and 145 to get 280, then divide by 2 to get 140. Forgetting the division is the classic slip, and 280 mEq/L should look wrong immediately because it sits far outside any plausible serum value.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A student finds that distilled water barely conducts current, while a 0.9% (w/v) NaCl solution - 0.9 g of NaCl per 100 mL - conducts strongly. What is the primary reason for the difference?

options.text: The roughly 9 g/L of NaCl dissociates into mobile hydrated Na+ and Cl- that serve as charge carriers
The roughly 9 g/L of NaCl stays as intact neutral units that drift toward the electrodes and carry charge
The dissolved NaCl depresses the freezing point, and solutions with lower freezing points conduct better
The dissolved NaCl raises the polarity of the water, letting the solvent itself transmit electrons

rationales.whyCorrect: Pure water self-ionizes only to about 1 x 10^-7 M, so it holds almost no charge carriers. A 0.9% (w/v) solution contains 0.9 g per 100 mL, and since 1 L is ten 100-mL portions, 0.9 x 10 = 9 g/L of NaCl, which dissolves and dissociates into hydrated Na+ and Cl- that migrate toward opposite electrodes and complete the circuit. Freezing-point depression is a consequence of dissolved particles rather than a mechanism of conduction, and adding salt does not make water conduct on its own.
rationales.eli10: Conduction in solution is migration of charged particles, not electron flow through the liquid. Distilled water has almost nothing charged in it, so there is nothing to migrate. Salt changes that in two steps: it dissolves, and then it dissociates into separate Na+ and Cl- that water molecules surround (hydrate) and keep apart. Note that dissolving alone is not enough - sugar dissolves just as well and still does not conduct, because its particles stay neutral. Percent w/v converts easily: 0.9 g per 100 mL is 9 g in the ten 100-mL portions that make a liter.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: One mole of glucose and one mole of NaCl are each dissolved in separate 1 L beakers of water. Which comparison of the resulting solutions is accurate?

options.text: Both solutions contain the same number of dissolved particles, because equal moles of solute were used
Glucose gives more dissolved particles, because its molecules split into smaller fragments in water
Neither solution conducts current, because both solids dissolve as intact electrically neutral units
NaCl gives twice as many dissolved particles as glucose, because it dissociates into Na+ and Cl-

rationales.whyCorrect: Glucose is a nonelectrolyte that dissolves as intact C6H12O6 molecules, giving 1 mol of particles per mole. NaCl is a strong electrolyte that dissociates into Na+ and Cl-, giving 2 mol of particles per mole, a ratio of 2/1 = 2. Glucose is a monosaccharide and does not hydrolyze into smaller units on dissolving. Because the NaCl solution contains ions it conducts, and because it contains twice the particles its osmolarity is about twice as high.
rationales.eli10: Separate two questions: how much solute went in, and how many independent particles came out. Both beakers received 1 mol of solute, so the first answer is identical. But glucose enters the water whole and stays whole - one molecule in, one particle in solution - while each NaCl formula unit separates into two particles, a sodium ion and a chloride ion. Particle count, not molecular size, is what determines osmolarity and other colligative properties, and the presence of charge on those particles is what determines conductivity.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A lab measures a 0.05 M KCl solution, then a 0.1 M KCl solution, using the same electrodes and temperature. Which change is expected, and by what factor does the mobile-ion concentration change?

options.text: Conductivity falls, because the extra dissolved ions interfere with one another and stop migrating
Conductivity rises by a factor of 4, because K+ and Cl- each double independently
Conductivity is essentially unchanged, because KCl yields the same two ion types at any concentration
Conductivity rises, because the concentration of mobile ions increases by a factor of 2

rationales.whyCorrect: For a strong electrolyte well below saturation, the number of charge carriers per liter scales directly with concentration, so 0.1/0.05 = 2 means both [K+] and [Cl-] double and conductivity rises roughly twofold. The two ion concentrations rise together as part of the same doubling; they do not multiply to give a fourfold effect. KCl is far below its solubility limit, so nothing precipitates, and ion-ion interference is negligible at these dilute concentrations.
rationales.eli10: Conductivity depends on how many charged particles per liter are available to migrate. Doubling the amount of KCl in the same volume doubles that supply: 0.1 divided by 0.05 equals 2. It is tempting to double once for K+ and again for Cl-, but those two are not independent - one doubling of KCl produces one doubling of the whole ion population, so the factor is 2, not 4. Crowding effects that reduce ion mobility do exist, but only at concentrations far higher than these.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Clinical laboratories often report electrolytes in milliequivalents rather than millimoles. For calcium, 1 mmol of Ca2+ corresponds to how many mEq, and what does that reveal about the two units?

options.text: 1 mEq, because milliequivalents and millimoles are alternative names for the same quantity
0.5 mEq, because equivalents divide the amount of substance by the magnitude of the charge
2 mEq, because equivalents weight each ion by the magnitude of the charge it carries
40 mEq, because equivalents are obtained by applying the molar mass of the element

rationales.whyCorrect: Milliequivalents equal millimoles multiplied by the absolute value of the ionic charge, so for the divalent Ca2+ ion 1 x 2 = 2 mEq. The equivalent expresses charge-combining capacity, which is why clinicians use it when comparing cations with anions for electroneutrality. Molar mass converts between mass and moles and plays no part in this conversion. For monovalent ions such as Na+ and K+ the two values coincide numerically, which is precisely why the distinction is easy to overlook.
rationales.eli10: Millimoles answer 'how many ions are present', while milliequivalents answer 'how much charge do they bring'. Those questions give the same number only when each ion carries exactly one charge. Calcium carries two, so a single millimole of it delivers 1 x 2 = 2 milliequivalents of positive charge. The direction matters: multiply by the charge, never divide, because a more highly charged ion supplies more charge, not less.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A hypothetical teaching solution contains 0.02 mol of KCl dissolved per liter of water. Assuming complete dissociation, what is the concentration of K+ expressed in mEq/L?

options.text: 2 mEq/L, because the amount in moles is divided by the charge on the potassium ion
20 mEq/L, because 0.02 mol/L equals 20 mmol/L and K+ carries a single positive charge
40 mEq/L, because the K+ and the Cl- released by each formula unit are both counted
0.02 mEq/L, because for a monovalent ion the equivalent concentration equals the molarity

rationales.whyCorrect: Two steps are required. Convert the unit prefix: 0.02 mol/L x 1000 = 20 mmol/L. Then multiply by the charge magnitude of 1 for K+, giving 20 mEq/L. Option D correctly notes that mmol/L and mEq/L coincide for monovalent ions but fails to convert mol/L to mmol/L first. Chloride is a distinct anion reported separately and is never folded into the potassium result.
rationales.eli10: Work the prefix and the charge as separate operations. The prefix: a millimole is one thousandth of a mole, so 0.02 mol/L becomes 20 mmol/L by multiplying by 1000. The charge: potassium is K+, one unit of charge, so multiplying by 1 leaves the value at 20 mEq/L. The equality of mmol/L and mEq/L for monovalent ions is a useful check, but it holds only after the amounts are in the same prefix - 0.02 and 20 are not interchangeable.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A hypothetical teaching solution is analyzed for four cations: Na+ 5 mmol/L, Mg2+ 2 mmol/L, K+ 4 mmol/L, and Ca2+ 3 mmol/L. Which cation contributes the most positive charge per liter, and how much?

options.text: Na+, contributing 5 mEq/L, because it is present at the highest millimolar concentration
Mg2+, contributing 4 mEq/L, because its double charge outweighs every other cation listed
K+, contributing 4 mEq/L, because monovalent ions dominate the charge total in solution
Ca2+, contributing 6 mEq/L, because its 3 mmol/L is doubled by its 2+ charge
